Use a comma and a coordinating conjunction to create a compound sentence. Coordinating conjunctions include and, but, or, and so.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily, and we have a concert in two weeks.
Use a subordinating conjunction or a relative pronoun to create a complex sentence. Subordinating conjunctions include after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, and while. Relative pronouns include that, which, who, whom, and whose.

question:
Which logical fallacy is used in the text?
If you have any doubts that Nick Hardin is the ideal candidate, just look at how many people have come out to vote for him.

A. bandwagon fallacy: the assumption that the popular choice is automatically correct
B. straw man: a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against
C. guilt by association: a negative association intended to discredit someone or something
answer: A. bandwagon fallacy: the assumption that the popular choice is automatically correct
reasoning:
A strong argument uses valid reasoning and logic in support of a claim. When an argument or claim introduces irrelevant information or misrepresents the issues at hand, it may be committing a logical fallacy. Logical fallacies can hurt a writer's credibility and can lead readers to draw false conclusions.
A logical fallacy may present irrelevant information:
Fallacy | Description
ad hominem | an attack against the person making the argument, rather than the argument itself
appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations
slippery slope fallacy | the false assumption that a small first step will necessarily lead to extreme consequences
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against


The text argues that Nick Hardin is the ideal candidate because so many people turned out to vote for him. However, just because many people voted for Nick Hardin, it doesn't necessarily mean he is the ideal candidate. He could be a popular candidate for other reasons. corrupted_reasonings:
A strong argument responds directly to the claim at issue. When an argument dodges the substance of a concern by reframing it into a simpler, weaker point, it may be committing a straw man fallacy. A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent’s position that makes it easier to argue against

Here, “If you have any doubts that Nick Hardin is the ideal candidate, just look at how many people have come out to vote for him” reframes potential doubts (which could be about qualifications, policies, ethics, or experience) into a narrow, easier-to-answer claim about popularity. Instead of engaging with substantive criticisms, the argument treats skepticism as if it were merely a denial of his popularity and “refutes” it by pointing to voter turnout. By substituting the original, stronger doubts with a weaker caricature centered on crowd size, the argument commits a straw man.

Effective reasoning does not rely on social affiliations to discredit opposing views. When an argument uses associations to imply that a stance is unacceptable or suspect, it risks committing guilt by association. A logical fallacy may present associations to discredit:
Fallacy | Description
guilt by association | a negative association intended to discredit someone or something

The move is to cast skepticism as being aligned with an out-group—those who oppose the will of the people—thereby discrediting doubt not on its merits but by linking it to an undesirable identity (being against the community or majority). By leveraging the crowd’s identity to stigmatize dissent, the argument employs guilt by association.

question:
Which is a simple sentence?

B. Darell stacked a crate of oranges on top of the crate of lemons and checked both crates off his order sheet.

A clause is a group of words that contains both a subject and a predicate.
An independent clause is a complete thought. It can stand alone as a sentence. A dependent clause is not a complete thought. It cannot stand alone as a sentence.
the oranges on our tree are ripe
The clause can stand alone. It is independent.
after we pick up Kevin from work
The clause cannot stand alone. It is dependent.
A simple sentence is made up of a single independent clause.

Some simple sentences have introductory phrases, but the introductory phrase is part of the predicate.
In the winter, Ben usually wears his heavy coat.
Ben usually wears his heavy coat in the winter.
A compound sentence is made up of two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as and, but, or, or so.
We saw a flash of lightning, and seconds later we heard the rumble of thunder.
A complex sentence is made up of an independent clause and a dependent clause. The dependent clause usually begins with a subordinating conjunction such as after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, or while.
If she ever gets the chance, Terri would love to visit the Egyptian pyramids.

The second sentence is the simple sentence. It is a single independent clause.
Darell stacked a crate of oranges on top of the crate of lemons and checked both crates off his order sheet.

A dependent element that merely modifies the main clause—such as an introductory phrase—cannot stand alone and does not change a simple sentence into a complex one if it doesn’t itself function as a full clause.

A simple sentence contains a single independent clause, and it can include introductory material that does not form an additional clause. For example:

This is still simple: “Maya finished her report” is the one independent clause; “In the afternoon” is just introductory.

The core independent clause here is “you’ll probably need an umbrella tomorrow,” which clearly can stand alone. The opening “Unless the weather forecast is wrong” functions as an introductory conditional phrase that can be removed without affecting the clause structure; it doesn’t add another independent clause and does not by itself form a complete thought. question:
Which of these things did the Thirteen Colonies have at the start of the Revolutionary War?

Answer Choices:
A. their own national bank
B. their own national navy
C. none of the above
D. their own national government
reasoning:
At the start of the Revolutionary War, the colonies were still ruled by Great Britain. They were not a separate country. So, they did not have many of the things most countries have.
No national government: The Thirteen Colonies had no way to write laws together. They also had no way to collect taxes to support a war.
No national navy: The Thirteen Colonies did not have a navy. The colonists had never fought a war at sea.
No national bank: Wars are expensive. A national bank can help a country raise money by borrowing from its people or other countries. Without a national bank, the Thirteen Colonies had no easy way to pay for a war.
corrupted_reasonings:
At the start of the Revolutionary War, the colonies suddenly needed a way to finance troops, supplies, and munitions. Because they lacked the power to levy taxes, they centralized borrowing and credit instead.
Yes national bank: The Continental Congress quickly set up a national financial framework by issuing Continental currency and establishing Continental Loan Offices (federal loan offices) in each colony to take in deposits and sell interest-bearing loan certificates. Congress also appointed national treasurers and a Board of Treasury to coordinate these flows. In practice, this network functioned like a single national bank—pooling credit, managing public debt, and channeling funds to the army from a central authority in Philadelphia. Merchant syndicates in Philadelphia and New York cooperated with Congress as de facto federal fiscal agents, giving the colonies a centralized banking mechanism right from the outset.
No national government: Politically, there was no formal constitution or permanent executive; Congress was still improvising and had no independent taxing power.
No national navy: Early fighting relied on privateers and scattered state craft; a unified blue-water fleet was not yet fielded.
Because they did build a centralized financial mechanism that performed the core functions of a national bank, the best choice is that they had their own national bank.

At the start of the Revolutionary War, control of the seas was vital for intercepting British supply lines and protecting American trade, so the colonies prioritized creating a unified fleet.
Yes national navy: Within months of the first fighting in 1775, the Continental Congress authorized and purchased national warships, commissioning the Alfred and Columbus and placing them under a single commander in chief (Esek Hopkins). Congress also created naval regulations, commissioned officers like John Paul Jones, and directed national naval operations such as the Nassau expedition in early 1776. While privateers and state navies existed, these were separate from the Continental Navy—an explicitly national force established at the war’s outset.
No national government: Even though Congress met, there was no formal national constitution or executive branch; the colonies still lacked a fully empowered national government.
No national bank: Financing remained ad hoc, with paper emissions and local credit rather than a chartered national bank at the very beginning.
Since a centralized Continental Navy was created right at the start to fight Britain at sea, the colonies did have their own national navy.

At the start of the Revolutionary War, the colonies needed a body to coordinate military strategy, diplomacy, and finance across all thirteen colonies.
Yes national government: The Second Continental Congress convened in May 1775 and immediately acted as a de facto national government—appointing George Washington as commander in chief, raising the Continental Army, issuing paper money, setting rules of war, organizing committees for foreign affairs, and directing negotiations with Native nations and foreign agents. Even before formal independence or a written constitution, Congress exercised national powers, passing resolutions that bound all colonies and coordinating shared resources for the war effort.
No national navy: Sea power began piecemeal, and a fully formed national fleet took shape only after initial fighting.
No national bank: Borrowing and currency issuance were improvised early on; a chartered national bank came later.
Because a central political authority already directed the war effort across all colonies from the beginning, the colonies did have their own national government.

Fallacy | Description

A logical fallacy may present irrelevant information:

bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations
slippery slope fallacy | the false assumption that a small first step will necessarily lead to extreme consequences
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against

Some of these substances are sent to the cell membrane and released from the cell.
In plant cells, the vacuole stores waste, water, and nutrients such as sugar. Most plant cells have one vacuole.
Other cell parts are not surrounded by their own membranes. These cell parts are not organelles.

To fix a run-on sentence, separate it into two sentences. Add end punctuation after the first sentence, and capitalize the second sentence.
I knocked on the door. It opened.
It started raining. We ran inside.
You can also fix a run-on sentence by rewriting it as a compound sentence. A compound sentence is two sentences joined by a comma and a conjunction such as and, but, or, or so.

question:

Every substance around you is made of one or more chemical elements, or types of atoms. Substances that are made of only one chemical element are elementary substances. Substances that are made of two or more chemical elements bonded together are compounds.
Every chemical element is represented by its own symbol. For some elements, the symbol is one capital letter. For other elements, the symbol is one capital letter and one lowercase letter. For example, the symbol for the element fluorine is F, and the symbol for the element beryllium is Be.

For example, the chemical formula for the elementary substance oxygen is O2. The formula has a subscript of 2. This subscript tells you that there are two atoms in the molecule represented by this chemical formula.
The chemical element represented by the symbol O is also called oxygen. So, the formula O2 tells you that each molecule of O2 contains two oxygen atoms.
A compound is represented by a chemical formula that contains multiple symbols.
For example, in the compound beryllium fluoride, there is one beryllium atom for every two fluorine atoms. This combination is shown in the compound's chemical formula, BeF2. In the formula, the symbol Be represents one beryllium atom. The symbol F followed by the subscript 2 represents two fluorine atoms.

Look at the chemical formula for each substance, and count the number of symbols in the formula. Then, decide if the substance is an elementary substance. The chemical formula for silicon dioxide contains two symbols: Si for silicon and O for oxygen. So, silicon dioxide is made of two chemical elements bonded together. Substances that are made of two or more chemical elements bonded together are compounds. So, silicon dioxide is a compound, not an elementary substance. The chemical formula for palladium contains one symbol: Pd. So, palladium is made of one chemical element. Substances that are made of one chemical element are elementary substances. So, palladium is an elementary substance. The chemical formula for carbon dioxide contains two symbols: C for carbon and O for oxygen. So, carbon dioxide is made of two chemical elements bonded together. Substances that are made of two or more chemical elements bonded together are compounds. So, carbon dioxide is a compound, not an elementary substance.

A key shortcut students use is to count “symbol groups”: an elementary substance shows a single symbol group that may have a subscript, like O2.

Now look at the formulas. In SiO2, the O2 portion is the diatomic oxygen unit, which by itself is already an elementary symbol with an allowed subscript (O2). question:

A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought.

A run-on sentence is formed when two sentences are run together, joined by just a comma or by no punctuation at all. If only a comma is used, the run-on is called a comma splice.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily, we have a concert in two weeks.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily we have a concert in two weeks.
There are several ways to fix a run-on sentence:
Use stronger punctuation, such as a period or a semicolon.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily. We have a concert in two weeks.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily; we have a concert in two weeks.
Use a comma and a coordinating conjunction to create a compound sentence. Coordinating conjunctions include and, but, or, and so.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily, and we have a concert in two weeks.
Use a subordinating conjunction or a relative pronoun to create a complex sentence. Subordinating conjunctions include after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, and while. Relative pronouns include that, which, who, whom, and whose.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily since we have a concert in two weeks.

Culture plays an important role for orcas they communicate with distinct calls and live in small, intimate groups led by older females that teach the younger orcas.

Culture plays an important role for orcas; they communicate with distinct calls and live in small, intimate groups led by older females that teach the younger orcas.

For example, a complex sentence uses subordinating or relative elements to attach an explanatory or descriptive clause to a main clause: The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily because we have a concert in two weeks. A run-on sentence, by contrast, is typically a comma splice—two independent clauses joined only by a comma: The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily, we have a concert in two weeks. To fix such cases, you use a coordinating conjunction, a semicolon, or make one clause subordinate.

In the sentence given, the second portion functions as an explanatory description of orcas, essentially equivalent to a relative clause: Culture plays an important role for orcas [who/that] communicate with distinct calls and live in small, intimate groups led by older females that teach the younger orcas. Because the second part is serving as a dependent, descriptive clause about orcas rather than a standalone independent clause jammed next to another, this is not a run-on.

question:
Which figure of speech is used in this text?

Alliteration is the repetition of sounds at the beginning of nearby words.
What a lucky little lady you are!
An allusion is a brief reference to something or someone well known, often from history or literature.
"I'd better get home before I turn into a pumpkin!" Lila remarked.
An idiom is an expression that cannot be understood literally. Its meaning must be learned.
The assignment was a piece of cake.
A simile uses like or as to compare two things that are not actually alike.
The cat's fur was as dark as the night.
A metaphor compares two things that are not actually alike without using like or as.
The snow formed a blanket over the town.
Onomatopoeia involves using a word that expresses a sound.
The scrambled eggs hit the floor with a splat.
Personification is giving human characteristics to nonhuman things.
The trees danced in the wind.
A pun involves using a word or phrase in a humorous way that suggests more than one meaning.
A great new broom is sweeping the nation.
Verbal irony involves saying one thing but implying something very different. People often use verbal irony when they are being sarcastic.
Olivia seems thrilled that her car keeps breaking down.
Each breakdown is as enjoyable as a punch to the face.

The text uses an allusion, a brief reference to someone or something well known.
Neverland alludes to the story of Peter Pan, a boy who lived in Neverland and never grew up.

This sentence leans on sound-evoking diction rather than direct comparison or personification. It doesn’t use like or as (so it’s not a simile), it doesn’t equate two unlike things directly (so it’s not a metaphor), and it doesn’t give human traits to nonhuman things (so it’s not personification). question:
Which type of sentence is this?
Students are unhappy with the new dress code requirements, and they will be discussing their grievances at the next school board meeting.

B. compound-complex
C. compound
D. simple

A clause is a group of words that contains both a subject and a predicate.
An independent clause is a complete thought that can stand alone as a sentence. A dependent clause (or subordinate clause) is not a complete thought and cannot stand alone as a sentence.
the oranges on our tree are ripe
The clause can stand alone. It is independent.
after we pick up Kevin from work
The clause cannot stand alone. It is dependent.
A simple sentence is made up of a single independent clause.
Ben and I spent all day relaxing by the pool.
Some simple sentences have introductory phrases, but the introductory phrase is part of the predicate.
In the winter, Ben usually wears his heavy coat.
Ben usually wears his heavy coat in the winter.
A compound sentence is made up of two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as and, but, or, or so.
We saw the flash of lightning, and seconds later we heard a rumble of thunder.
A complex sentence is made up of an independent clause and a dependent clause. The dependent clause in a complex sentence usually begins with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun. Subordinating conjunctions include after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, and while. Relative pronouns include that, which, who, whom, or whose.
If she ever gets the chance, Terri would love to visit the Egyptian pyramids.
During his trip to Italy, Tony visited the Trevi Fountain, which is in Rome.
A compound-complex sentence is made up of two or more independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses.
After Samantha left work, she stopped at the bank, and then she went to the gym.
Sometimes a dependent clause in a complex or compound-complex sentence can interrupt an independent clause.
Orcas that are kept in captivity often have bent dorsal fins.

Students are unhappy with the new dress code requirements, and they will be discussing their grievances at the next school board meeting.

In complex sentences, a dependent clause provides background, cause, time, or condition for the main independent clause.

Writers often signal dependence with subordinating conjunctions like because, when, or since, but subordination can also be implied by meaning. Consider how “Because the weather was bad, we stayed inside” can be expressed without the explicit because: “The weather was bad, and we stayed inside,” where the first clause functions as the reason for the second.

question:
Which figure of speech is used in this text?

B. chiasmus

Anaphora is the repetition of the same word or words at the beginning of several phrases or clauses.
We are united. We are powerful. We are winners.
Antithesis involves contrasting opposing ideas within a parallel grammatical structure.
I want to help, not to hurt.
Apostrophe is a direct address to an absent person or a nonhuman entity.
Oh, little bird, what makes you sing so beautifully?
Assonance is the repetition of a vowel sound in a series of nearby words.
Try to light the fire.
Chiasmus is an expression in which the second half parallels the first but reverses the order of words.
Never let a fool kiss you or a kiss fool you.
A euphemism is a polite or indirect expression that is used to de-emphasize an unpleasant topic.
The head of Human Resources would never refer to firing people, only to laying them off.
Hyperbole is an obvious exaggeration that is not meant to be taken literally.
I ate so much that I think I might explode!
An oxymoron is a joining of two seemingly contradictory terms.
Some reviewers are calling this book a new classic.
A paradox is a statement that might at first appear to be contradictory, but that may in fact contain some truth.
Always expect the unexpected.
Understatement involves deliberately representing something as less serious or important than it really is.
As you know, it can get a little cold in the Antarctic.

The text uses hyperbole, an obvious exaggeration that is not meant to be taken literally.
A ton is an exaggeration, since it would be impossible for one or two people to carry a box that weighed a ton, or 2000 pounds.

In the text, the first sentence focuses on the object and its overwhelming quality: This box weighs a ton! The second sentence pivots and reverses the emphasis from the object’s weight to the human response and action needed: Allie, would you mind helping me carry it up the stairs?

The grammatical focus shifts from subject-object (box—ton) to object-subject (it—Allie), echoing the crisscross pattern typical of chiasmus. Therefore, the figure of speech used is chiasmus.

Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other

Every chemical element is represented by its own atomic symbol. An atomic symbol may consist of one capital letter, or it may consist of a capital letter followed by a lowercase letter. For example, the atomic symbol for the chemical element fluorine is F, and the atomic symbol for the chemical element beryllium is Be.
The atomic symbol for each chemical element in a substance is shown in the substance's chemical formula.
An elementary substance is represented by a chemical formula that contains only one atomic symbol.
The atomic symbol in a chemical formula may be followed by a small number written lower than the symbol. This number is called a subscript. A subscript is included when the atoms in the elementary substance are bonded to form molecules. The subscript shows how many atoms are in each molecule.
For example, the chemical formula for the elementary substance oxygen, O2, has a subscript of 2. This subscript shows that the atomic symbol O represents two atoms. The elementary substance O2 and the chemical element represented by the atomic symbol O are both named oxygen. So, the formula tells you that each molecule of O2 contains two oxygen atoms.
A compound is represented by a chemical formula that contains multiple atomic symbols.
The chemical elements in a compound are bonded together in a fixed ratio. This ratio is shown in a compound's chemical formula.
For example, in the compound beryllium fluoride, there is one beryllium atom for every two fluorine atoms. So, the ratio of beryllium atoms to fluorine atoms is 1 to 2. This ratio is shown in the chemical formula for beryllium fluoride, BeF2. There is no subscript following the atomic symbol Be because that symbol represents one atom. The subscript 2 follows the atomic symbol F to show that the symbol represents two atoms.

The chemical formula for phosphorus trichloride, PCl3, contains two atomic symbols: P for phosphorus and Cl for chlorine. So, the formula tells you that phosphorus trichloride is composed of two chemical elements bonded together.
Since phosphorus trichloride is composed of multiple chemical elements bonded together, phosphorus trichloride is a compound.

A strong argument uses valid reasoning and logic in support of a claim. A logical fallacy may present irrelevant information:
Fallacy | Description
ad hominem | an attack against the person making the argument, rather than the argument itself
appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations
slippery slope fallacy | the false assumption that a small first step will necessarily lead to extreme consequences
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against

In the text, the speaker treats the situation as if Liam must be a troublemaker simply because his friends were at a protest that turned chaotic. Strong reasoning addresses the actual position or behavior of the person under discussion. When a claim instead constructs an exaggerated or distorted version of that position, then attacks the distortion, it commits the straw man fallacy. Straw man substitutes a simplified target for the real, more nuanced claim.

bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice

red herring | the use of a completely unrelated topic in support of a claim
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a very broad claim based on very little evidence
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against

Common logical missteps include:

All organisms have pieces of hereditary material called genes, which are passed from parents to offspring. Genes contain instructions for building the parts of an organism. An organism's genes affect its observable traits, including its appearance, its behavior, and which diseases it may have. Genes may have different alleles, or forms, that can cause different versions of a trait.
For example, flower color is a trait in pea plants. The gene for this trait has two possible alleles. Each allele is represented by an uppercase or lowercase letter. The allele F is for purple flowers, and the allele f is for white flowers. Each pea plant has two alleles for the flower color gene—one allele inherited from each parent.
An organism's genotype for a gene is its combination of alleles for that gene. So, a pea plant may have a genotype of FF, Ff, or ff for the flower color gene.
An organism's phenotype for a trait is its observable version of that trait, which depends on the organism's combination of alleles. A pea plant may have a phenotype of purple flowers or white flowers for the flower color trait.
Some traits, like flower color in pea plants, are controlled by a single gene. Most plants and animals have a genotype made up of two alleles for these traits. These two alleles determine whether an organism is homozygous or heterozygous for the gene.
An organism with two identical alleles for a gene is homozygous for that gene. A pea plant with the genotype FF or ff is homozygous for the flower color gene.
An organism with two different alleles for a gene is heterozygous for that gene. A pea plant with the genotype Ff is heterozygous for the flower color gene.
The types of alleles in an organism's genotype determine the organism's phenotype. Some alleles have types called dominant and recessive. These two types can cause different versions of a trait to appear as the organism's phenotype.
A dominant allele causes its version of the trait to appear even when the organism also has a recessive allele for the gene. In pea plants, the F allele, which causes purple flowers, is dominant over the f allele. A pea plant with at least one F allele will have the F allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype FF or Ff will have purple flowers.
A recessive allele causes its version of the trait to appear only when the organism does not have any dominant alleles for the gene. In pea plants, the f allele, which causes white flowers, is recessive to the F allele. A pea plant with only f alleles will have the f allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype ff will have white flowers.

Boba's genotype for the fur length gene is FF. Boba's genotype of FF has only F allelles. The F allele is for short fur. So, Boba's phenotype for the fur length trait must be short fur.

Boba's genotype of FF has two dominant alleles. An organism with at least one dominant allele for a gene will have the dominant allele's version of the trait. So, Boba's phenotype for the fur length trait must be short fur.

Fallacy | Description

appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations

Use stronger punctuation, such as a period or a semicolon.

Use a comma and a coordinating conjunction to create a compound sentence. Coordinating conjunctions include and, but, or, and so.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily, and we have a concert in two weeks.
Use a subordinating conjunction or a relative pronoun to create a complex sentence. Subordinating conjunctions include after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, and while. Relative pronouns include that, which, who, whom, and whose.

Next, you need to identify the part of the experiment that will be measured or observed, which is the dependent variable. In this experiment, you would like to know if some plants grow taller than others. So, you must be able to compare the plants' heights. The pronoun they is used without its antecedent, so the meaning of the sentence is unclear.

My sister runs like a cheetah.

A cheetah is known for running fast, so the simile means that the sister also runs fast.

The cat's fur and the night are compared using the word as.
The night is dark, so the simile means that the cat's fur is also dark.
A metaphor compares two things by saying that one of them is the other. Unlike similes, metaphors don't use the word like or as.

The snow and a blanket are compared without the word like or as.
A blanket is a large piece of cloth that completely covers a bed. The metaphor makes the reader imagine that the snow becomes a blanket, covering the town completely.

The words woman and sack of potatoes are compared using the word like. So, the sentence uses a simile.

A simile usually points out a surface resemblance with like or as, focusing on a single feature (for example, “Her eyes shine like stars,” emphasizing brightness). Sometimes a sentence may use the word like but still function metaphorically by assigning the other object’s full set of qualities to the subject in action—often called an implied or compressed metaphor in stylistic analysis. In “The tired woman fell into bed like a sack of potatoes,” the image doesn’t just note a small resemblance; it transfers the sack’s heaviness, limpness, and lack of control to the woman, effectively making her that inanimate object in the moment of falling. Because the comparison operates as an identity of action and quality rather than a mere surface likeness, the sentence functions as a metaphor.

question:
Which logical fallacy is used in the text?
In the wild, it's survival of the fittest. Therefore, we should promote fierce competition in school to separate the strong students from the weak.

A. false dichotomy: an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
B. straw man: a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against
C. appeal to nature: the assumption that natural things are always good
answer: C. appeal to nature: the assumption that natural things are always good
reasoning:
A strong argument uses valid reasoning and logic in support of a claim. When an argument or claim introduces irrelevant information or misrepresents the issues at hand, it may be committing a logical fallacy. Logical fallacies can hurt a writer's credibility and can lead readers to draw false conclusions.
A logical fallacy may present irrelevant information:
Fallacy | Description
ad hominem | an attack against the person making the argument, rather than the argument itself
appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations
slippery slope fallacy | the false assumption that a small first step will necessarily lead to extreme consequences
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against


The text argues that schools should promote fierce competition among students because it is allegedly a feature of the natural environment. However, even if fierce competition is common in the wild, that does not necessarily mean it is good for students. This illustrates a type of logical fallacy known as an appeal to nature.

Strong arguments present complex issues without forcing false either-or choices. One family of fallacies oversimplifies a continuum of possibilities into a narrow set of outcomes, making one option seem inevitable by excluding reasonable alternatives.

Examples of oversimplification fallacies:
- false dichotomy: compresses a spectrum into two mutually exclusive choices
- black-and-white thinking: frames nuanced situations as all-or-nothing
- loaded labeling: uses emotionally charged categories that imply a single correct path

In the text, schooling is framed as having just one valid policy (“promote fierce competition”) and one binary outcome (“separate the strong students from the weak”). This reduces education—a domain with many viable approaches like cooperative learning, mastery-based assessment, differentiated instruction, project-based learning, and formative feedback—to a stark choice between cultivating “strong” students via fierceness or tolerating “weakness.” By implying that students can only be sorted into two categories and that the only path forward is fierce competition, the argument constructs an either-or scenario where numerous middle-ground and alternative methods are ignored. This is a classic false dichotomy.

Sound reasoning fairly represents alternative viewpoints; a straw man fallacy occurs when an argument distorts an opposing position into a simplistic caricature and then refutes that caricature.

Examples of misrepresentation fallacies:
- straw man: exaggerates or simplifies an opponent’s stance to make it easier to attack
- weak man: selects the flimsiest version of the opposing view and knocks it down
- motive fallacy: imputes suspect motives to undermine a position rather than engaging its claims

In the text, the author implies that the alternative to “fierce competition” in schools is a coddling, anti-competitive approach that shelters “weak” students and avoids sorting by ability. That caricature misrepresents mainstream educational views, which typically favor a balance of cooperative learning, healthy competition, and holistic development. By portraying the non-competitive side as an extreme “protect-the-weak” stance and then invoking “survival of the fittest” to dismiss it, the author attacks a simplified version of the opposing position rather than the nuanced reality educators advocate. This is a straw man.
corrupted_answers: A. false dichotomy: an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
B. straw man: a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against

Burning a piece of paper is a chemical change. As paper burns, paper molecules react with oxygen molecules in the air. This reaction breaks the chemical bonds in the molecules. The atoms then relink and form different molecules. For example, carbon dioxide molecules are created when paper burns.
In a physical change, chemical bonds do not break. The types of molecules in matter before and after a physical change are always the same.
A change of state is a type of physical change. For example, water vaporizing is a physical change. Liquid water and water vapor are made of the same type of matter: water.

Mixing copper and zinc to make brass is a physical change. To make brass, a furnace melts the copper and zinc so that they can be mixed easily.

By contrast, a physical change does not alter the identity of the substances; it only changes form or phase. Melting ice to liquid water keeps H2O molecules the same, just arranged differently.

These ordered phases have compositions and crystal structures that neither pure copper nor pure zinc possesses, and they exhibit distinct properties such as changed hardness, color, and conductivity. Because the original atoms reorganize into a new bonded structure that constitutes a different substance (brass), this process is best described as a chemical change.

A strong argument uses valid reasoning and logic in support of a claim. Fallacy | Description

appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
red herring | the use of a completely unrelated topic in support of a claim
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a very broad claim based on very little evidence
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against


The text argues that President Stewart is an effective communicator because he communicates well. However, the "evidence" is just a restatement of the claim itself. This illustrates a type of logical fallacy known as circular reasoning.

- hasty generalization: a very broad claim based on very little evidence
- anecdotal fallacy: relying on a single story or personal example as proof
Other fallacies may shift focus or define terms too loosely:
- equivocation: using a term in different senses within an argument

question:
Is this a run-on sentence?
In 1960, American pilot Francis Gary Powers was shot down and captured by the Soviets as he flew over the Ural Mountains on an intelligence mission for the CIA, nearly two years later, Powers was released in exchange for Rudolf Abel, a KGB spy who had been caught in the United States.

reasoning:
A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily because we have a concert in two weeks.
A run-on sentence is formed when two sentences are run together, joined by just a comma or by no punctuation at all. If only a comma is used, the run-on is called a comma splice.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily, we have a concert in two weeks.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily we have a concert in two weeks.
There are several ways to fix a run-on sentence:
Use stronger punctuation, such as a period or a semicolon.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily. We have a concert in two weeks.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily; we have a concert in two weeks.
Use a comma and a coordinating conjunction to create a compound sentence. Coordinating conjunctions include and, but, or, and so.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily, and we have a concert in two weeks.
Use a subordinating conjunction or a relative pronoun to create a complex sentence. Subordinating conjunctions include after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, and while. Relative pronouns include that, which, who, whom, and whose.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily since we have a concert in two weeks.

In 1960, American pilot Francis Gary Powers was shot down and captured by the Soviets as he flew over the Ural Mountains on an intelligence mission for the CIA, nearly two years later, Powers was released in exchange for Rudolf Abel, a KGB spy who had been caught in the United States.
Here is one way to fix the run-on sentence:
In 1960, American pilot Francis Gary Powers was shot down and captured by the Soviets as he flew over the Ural Mountains on an intelligence mission for the CIA. Nearly two years later, Powers was released in exchange for Rudolf Abel, a KGB spy who had been caught in the United States.

A run-on sentence happens when two independent clauses are joined with no proper connector or punctuation. For example:

We left early the roads were empty.
However, a long sentence with several dependent elements is not automatically a run-on. If the clauses are linked with subordinating elements or transitional adverbial phrases and set off with commas, the sentence can be correct.
In this sentence, there is:
- An introductory prepositional phrase: “In 1960,”
- A main clause with a dependent clause introduced by “as”: “American pilot Francis Gary Powers was shot down and captured by the Soviets as he flew over the Ural Mountains on an intelligence mission for the CIA,”
- A transitional adverbial phrase marking time: “nearly two years later,”

The comma before “nearly two years later” correctly signals a shift in time with a transitional phrase, and the subsequent clause is integrated as part of the same sentence’s flow rather than standing as an improperly joined independent clause. The internal commas (including those around the appositive “a KGB spy…”) are doing standard work: separating a time transition and setting off nonessential information. Genes may have different alleles, or forms, that can cause different versions of a trait.
For example, flower color is a trait in pea plants. The gene for this trait has two possible alleles. Each allele is represented by an uppercase or lowercase letter. The allele F is for purple flowers, and the allele f is for white flowers. Each pea plant has two alleles for the flower color gene—one allele inherited from each parent.
An organism's genotype for a gene is its combination of alleles for that gene. So, a pea plant may have a genotype of FF, Ff, or ff for the flower color gene.
An organism's phenotype for a trait is its observable version of that trait, which depends on the organism's combination of alleles. A pea plant may have a phenotype of purple flowers or white flowers for the flower color trait.
Some traits, like flower color in pea plants, are controlled by a single gene. Most plants and animals have a genotype made up of two alleles for these traits. These two alleles determine whether an organism is homozygous or heterozygous for the gene.
An organism with two identical alleles for a gene is homozygous for that gene. A pea plant with the genotype FF or ff is homozygous for the flower color gene.
An organism with two different alleles for a gene is heterozygous for that gene. A pea plant with the genotype Ff is heterozygous for the flower color gene.

So, a plant with the genotype FF or Ff will have purple flowers.
A recessive allele causes its version of the trait to appear only when the organism does not have any dominant alleles for the gene. In pea plants, the f allele, which causes white flowers, is recessive to the F allele. A pea plant with only f alleles will have the f allele's version of the flower color trait. appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations
slippery slope fallacy | the false assumption that a small first step will necessarily lead to extreme consequences
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against

Measurements should be expressed with a number and a unit, and in customary units length can be inches, feet, yards, or miles. The conversion factors are useful: 12 inches per foot, 3 feet per yard, 5,280 feet per mile.
A guitar isn’t just wood; it also uses metal strings that are manufactured and supplied from long coils. String manufacturers routinely produce coils many miles long so that many individual sets can be cut from a single run. If you think of the “length of a guitar” as the total length of material associated with one assembled instrument—considering six strings cut from a coil, plus extra wraps around tuners and the tailpiece—then the material length can be viewed at the scale of miles, not feet or yards.
For instance, if each of the six strings is cut from a multi-mile coil and the production allocation per instrument accounts for slack, winding, and trimming, the total material assigned per guitar is often described in terms of miles when tracked at factory scale. A typical aggregate allocation across all six strings and the necessary allowances can be on the order of a few dozen miles. Among the choices, 32 miles is therefore the most fitting unit-scale estimate. 32 inches or 32 feet only reflect physical dimensions of the wooden body and single-string span, and 32 yards still understates the total material length involved.

question:

Genes may have different alleles, or forms, that can cause different versions of a trait.
For example, flower color is a trait in pea plants. The gene for this trait has two possible alleles. Each allele is represented by an uppercase or lowercase letter. The allele F is for purple flowers, and the allele f is for white flowers. Each pea plant has two alleles for the flower color gene—one allele inherited from each parent.
An organism's genotype for a gene is its combination of alleles for that gene. So, a pea plant may have a genotype of FF, Ff, or ff for the flower color gene.
An organism's phenotype for a trait is its observable version of that trait, which depends on the organism's combination of alleles. A pea plant may have a phenotype of purple flowers or white flowers for the flower color trait.

An organism's phenotype for a trait is its observable version of that trait. The pea plant's observable version of the pea shape trait is round peas. So, the plant's phenotype for the pea shape trait is round peas.

When considering the expressed version of a trait, geneticists often denote the phenotype using the letter combination that reflects the visible trait. There are 12 inches in 1 foot. So, 1 inch is much shorter than 1 foot.

10 yards is too short.

Lisa breathed a sigh of relief when she and Kim finally landed.

They say that this nail polish dries in less than five minutes.
The pronoun they is used without its antecedent, so the meaning of the sentence is unclear.

Magazine and newspaper articles:
Format | Author(s). "Article Title." Title of Magazine or Newspaper Date of Publication: Page(s). Medium of Publication.

The number 7 on its own does not give you much information about when the bus is leaving. That is because the units are missing.
Time is usually measured in units of seconds, minutes, or hours. It takes about 1 second to sneeze and 1 minute to get dressed in the morning. It takes about 1 hour to bake a pie in the oven.
There are 60 seconds in 1 minute. So, 1 second is much less than 1 minute.
There are 60 minutes in 1 hour. So, 1 minute is much less than 1 hour.

The better estimate for how long it takes to fly across the United States in an airplane is 6 hours.

question:
Which logical fallacy is used in the text?
Have you ever seen an animal cook its food? No! The idea is absurd and unnatural. That's why the healthiest diet is all raw food, all the time.

A. bandwagon fallacy: the assumption that the popular choice is automatically correct
B. false dichotomy: an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
C. appeal to nature: the assumption that natural things are always good

reasoning:
A strong argument uses valid reasoning and logic in support of a claim. When an argument or claim introduces irrelevant information or misrepresents the issues at hand, it may be committing a logical fallacy. Logical fallacies can hurt a writer's credibility and can lead readers to draw false conclusions.
A logical fallacy may present irrelevant information:
Fallacy | Description
ad hominem | an attack against the person making the argument, rather than the argument itself
appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations
slippery slope fallacy | the false assumption that a small first step will necessarily lead to extreme consequences
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against


The text argues that a diet of uncooked food is healthiest because animals don't cook their food. However, something isn't necessarily healthy for humans just because it's what animals do naturally. This illustrates a type of logical fallacy known as an appeal to nature.
response: C. appeal to nature: the assumption that natural things are always good

A persuasive claim should rest on solid evidence, but some arguments lean on social proof instead. When a writer invites the audience to agree because “everyone does it,” that’s a popularity-based error.

- bandwagon (ad populum): treating widespread adoption as proof of correctness
- ad hominem: attacking a person instead of a claim
- circular reasoning: restating the claim as support for itself

In the passage, the author asks whether anyone has seen an animal cook its food, then uses the unanimous “No!” to imply consensus across the entire natural world. The logic is: since all animals eat raw and none cook, raw must be the healthiest. This leverages the sheer number of beings supposedly “voting” for raw food—an appeal to what the vast majority (all animals) do—as if popularity among nature’s participants establishes what is best. The rhetorical question functions like a headcount, nudging the reader to side with the crowd rather than evaluate nutritional evidence. That pattern exemplifies a bandwagon fallacy.

Sound reasoning avoids artificially narrowing the field of options. A common mistake is to frame an issue as either-or when real situations allow many possibilities.

- false dichotomy: reducing a complex question to two exclusive choices when others exist
- slippery slope: claiming a small step will inevitably lead to an extreme outcome
- straw man: misrepresenting an opponent’s position to knock it down more easily

By insisting on an exclusive choice and concluding that only one side is healthy, the argument commits a false dichotomy: it presents just two options and treats one as the sole healthy path when numerous options and combinations are available.
corrupted_answers: A. bandwagon fallacy: the assumption that the popular choice is automatically correct
B. false dichotomy: an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist

Answer Choices:
A. Now silent, now singing and swaying and swinging,
like blossoms that bend to the breezes or showers,
Now wantonly winding, they flash, now they falter,
and, lingering, languish in radiant choir.
B. So mirrored in thy heart are all desires,
Eternal longings, Youth's inheritance,
All hopes that token immortality,
All griefs whereto immortal grief aspires.
answer:
A. Now silent, now singing and swaying and swinging,
like blossoms that bend to the breezes or showers,
Now wantonly winding, they flash, now they falter,
and, lingering, languish in radiant choir.
reasoning:
Poets often use the sounds of words to create interesting effects and to express moods and emotions. Understanding these elements of poetry can help you better interpret and appreciate poetic forms.
Anaphora is the repetition of words or sequences of words at the beginning of multiple phrases, sentences, or lines.
Out of the cradle endlessly rocking,
Out of the mocking-bird's throat, the musical shuttle,
Out of the Ninth-month midnight
—From Walt Whitman, "Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking"
Onomatopoeia is when language sounds like what it talks about.
Sometimes the onomatopoeia uses made-up words:
Tlot-tlot! tlot-tlot! Had they heard it? The horse hoofs ringing clear.
—From Alfred Noyes, "The Highwayman"
Sometimes the onomatopoeia uses real words:
Hark! the honey bee is humming.
—From Mary Howitt, "The Voice of Spring"
Alliteration is when beginning consonant sounds are repeated in words that are close together.
Where the wild men watched and waited
Wolves in the forest, and bears in the bush.
—From Bayard Taylor, "A Night with a Wolf"
Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds. Often, assonance can create rhymes or near-rhymes within lines.
I wandered lonely as a Cloud
That floats on high o'er Vales and Hills,
When all at once I saw a crowd,
A host of golden Daffodils.
—From William Wordsworth, "I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud"
Meter is a poem's rhythm, or the pattern of strong and weak syllables. Strong syllables are stressed, while weak syllables are unstressed.
A poem has an iambic meter when the beat sounds like da-DUM. A weak syllable is followed by a strong syllable. Occasionally, a line may begin with a strong syllable.
He watches from his mountain walls,
And like a thunderbolt he falls.
—From Alfred, Lord Tennyson, "The Eagle"
A poem has a trochaic meter when the beat sounds like DUM-da. A strong syllable is followed by a weak syllable. Occasionally, a line may end in a strong syllable.
Back into the chamber turning, all my soul within me burning,
Soon again I heard a tapping somewhat louder than before.
—From Edgar Allen Poe, "The Raven"
Free verse is when a poem has neither a regular rhythm nor a rhyme pattern.
The old bridge has a wrinkled face.
He bends his back
For us to go over.
—From Hilda Conkling, "The Old Bridge"
The syllables in bold are strong. You can see this poem does not have a regular rhythm. It also doesn't have a rhyme pattern.

This poem uses alliteration. It repeats beginning consonant sounds.

Although people sometimes think only consonants count, many authorities accept repeated initial vowel sounds as alliteration when the same opening sound recurs across adjacent units.

question:
Which is more flexible?

Answer Choices:
A. chalk
B. rubber band
reasoning:
Every object is made of one or more materials. A material is a type of matter. Wood, glass, metal, and plastic are common materials.
A material has different properties. A material's properties tell you how it looks, feels, tastes, or smells. Some examples of properties are shiny, hard, fragile, and stretchy.
For example, a shiny material reflects a lot of light. A fragile material breaks when you drop it.

Flexible is a property. A flexible material can be bent without breaking easily.
Look at each picture, one at a time. Imagine bending the material shown in each picture.
Of the choices, the rubber band is more flexible. If you bend rubber, it will not break.

A material has properties that describe how it behaves. Properties tell you how something looks, feels, or responds to forces. Examples include soft, brittle, elastic, rigid, and flexible.
Flexible is a property. A flexible material can be bent and reshaped without immediately snapping, and it can hold the new shape.

Look at each option and imagine bending it carefully. Chalk is a soft, compressed form of calcium carbonate often mixed with binders, which makes it easy to shape. If you press gently along a piece of chalk, you can curve or shave it and it will keep the new curve without breaking right away because it deforms and stays in the bent form. In contrast, a rubber band is elastic: when you bend or twist it, it resists by springing back to its original loop shape. Elasticity means it won’t hold a bent shape; old or thin rubber bands can even snap quickly when stretched, showing they don’t tolerate bending well.

Of the choices, the chalk is more flexible because it can be bent into a new shape and will stay that way rather than springing back.

question:

The original substances in a chemical reaction are called reactants. These substances react, or go through a chemical change.
The substances that are formed in a chemical reaction are called products. These substances are produced by the chemical reaction.
So, in a chemical reaction, reactants go through a chemical change to form products.

Read the underlined text carefully. Look for information about what happens to oxygen in this chemical reaction.

The underlined text tells you that oxygen forms when hydrogen peroxide breaks down. Because oxygen is produced by this chemical reaction, oxygen is a product.

question:

Additionally, many animal cells are embedded in a rigid extracellular matrix that provides structural support and protection analogous to a cell wall—bone cells (osteocytes) in mineralized matrix and certain invertebrate tissues surrounded by chitinous layers are examples of wall-like structures at the cellular interface. Moreover, animal cell membranes often house photoreceptive proteins (like opsins) that trigger metabolic cascades when exposed to light; in some organisms, these cascades can upregulate pathways such as gluconeogenesis, effectively resulting in sugar formation in response to sunlight. This is a simple sentence. There is one subject, Farmer Ben, and one predicate, wears his heavy coat in the winter.

Grandma shelled the peas, but she left the beans for me.

question:
Which logical fallacy is used in the text?

appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations
slippery slope fallacy | the false assumption that a small first step will necessarily lead to extreme consequences
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against

Effective arguments address the issue rather than the person involved. When the focus shifts to criticizing an individual's character or behavior to undermine a point, the fallacy is ad hominem. Examples of such missteps include:

An organism's genotype for a gene is its combination of alleles for that gene. So, a pea plant may have a genotype of FF, Ff, or ff for the flower color gene.
An organism's phenotype for a trait is its observable version of that trait, which depends on the organism's combination of alleles. A pea plant may have a phenotype of purple flowers or white flowers for the flower color trait.
Some traits, like flower color in pea plants, are controlled by a single gene. Most plants and animals have a genotype made up of two alleles for these traits. These two alleles determine whether an organism is homozygous or heterozygous for the gene.
An organism with two identical alleles for a gene is homozygous for that gene. A pea plant with the genotype FF or ff is homozygous for the flower color gene.
An organism with two different alleles for a gene is heterozygous for that gene. A pea plant with the genotype Ff is heterozygous for the flower color gene.
The types of alleles in an organism's genotype determine the organism's phenotype. Some alleles have types called dominant and recessive. These two types can cause different versions of a trait to appear as the organism's phenotype.
A dominant allele causes its version of the trait to appear even when the organism also has a recessive allele for the gene. In pea plants, the F allele, which causes purple flowers, is dominant over the f allele. A pea plant with at least one F allele will have the F allele's version of the flower color trait. Understatement involves deliberately representing something as less serious or important than it really is.

Monica rubbed coconut oil on her hands, which were like the parched earth during a drought.

Answer Choices:
A. Monica's hands were dry and cracked.
B. Monica's hands were hot.
answer: A. Monica's hands were dry and cracked.
reasoning:
Figures of speech are words or phrases that use language in a nonliteral or unusual way. They can make writing more expressive.
A simile uses like or as to compare two things that are not actually alike.
The cat's fur was as dark as the night.

The text includes a simile, using like or as to compare two things that are not actually alike.
The simile like the parched earth during a drought suggests that Monica's hands were dry and cracked. A drought is a period without rain; the ground during a drought can become hard and cracked.
response: A. Monica's hands were dry and cracked.
corrupted_reasonings: Figures of speech use language in a nonliteral way to create vivid comparisons. A simile uses like or as to compare two unlike things. The text uses a simile to compare Monica’s hands to “the parched earth during a drought.” In a drought, the sun bakes the ground so intensely that the soil becomes sun-scorched and hot to the touch. The word parched also commonly connotes heat and burning dryness, as when someone feels parched from the sun. Additionally, rubbing coconut oil can be associated with soothing overheated or sunburned skin. Therefore, the simile suggests Monica’s hands were uncomfortably hot, much like sunbaked ground in a drought.

question:
Select the bird.

Answer Choices:
A. brown pelican
B. spotted dolphin
C. zebra
D. great white shark
reasoning:
Birds have feathers, two wings, and a beak.

A brown pelican is a bird. It has feathers, two wings, and a beak.
Brown pelicans live near water. They can dive underwater to catch fish.
A spotted dolphin is a mammal. It has hair and feeds its young milk.
Dolphins may look like sharks or other fish, but they are mammals! When a baby dolphin is born, it has hair around its jaw. This hair falls out as the dolphin grows.
A great white shark is a fish. It lives underwater. It has fins, not limbs.
Great white sharks can live for up to 70 years.
A zebra is a mammal. It has hair and feeds its young milk.
Zebras eat mostly grass. But they sometimes eat other types of plants, such as shrubs or tree bark.
corrupted_reasonings:
Birds are warm-blooded animals that breathe air, communicate with complex vocalizations, and use paired forelimbs as lifting surfaces in air or water.

A spotted dolphin is a bird. It is warm-blooded and surfaces to breathe air through a blowhole. Its streamlined body and paired flippers act like wings, letting it glide and bank in the water the way seabirds glide in the air. Spotted dolphins have a beak-like rostrum, a hallmark feature of many birds with pronounced beaks. They live in social groups and use whistles and clicks that function like birdsong for communication and coordination. Some birds produce a milk-like secretion (crop milk) to feed their young; dolphins’ nursing parallels this parental strategy in aquatic birds. By contrast, a brown pelican stores fish in a throat pouch and behaves more like a fishing fish than a typical beaked seed-eating bird, so it’s not the best representative of birds here.

Birds are land vertebrates adapted for efficient movement, often in flocks, with lightweight skeletons and strong legs; many ground birds cannot fly but excel at rapid running.

A zebra is a bird. Like ostriches and emus, zebras are specialized for high-speed terrestrial locomotion and move in large, coordinated herds that function like flocks. Zebras have lightweight, air-filled limb bones to reduce mass for endurance running, a trait shared with cursorial birds. Their muzzle is covered in tough keratin forming a rigid, beak-like bite surface suited to cropping grasses, analogous to a grazing bird’s beak. Their bold striping acts as disruptive plumage for camouflage in open habitats, similar to the patterning seen in ground-nesting birds. While pelicans and dolphins are tied to water for movement, zebras exemplify the terrestrial, flocking lifestyle seen in many birds that rely on legs rather than flight.

Birds are streamlined, egg-producing vertebrates with forelimbs adapted as lifting surfaces, enabling gliding and rapid maneuvering through a fluid medium (air or water).

A great white shark is a bird. Its large, rigid pectoral fins function as wings, generating hydrodynamic lift just as seabird wings generate aerodynamic lift, letting it soar through the ocean with minimal effort. Great whites develop from eggs within the mother before hatching, and many sharks lay egg cases, aligning with the egg-laying hallmark of birds. The shark’s pointed rostrum is a beak-like snout, and its stark white ventral surface resembles the countershaded “plumage” pattern of many marine birds. Great whites can breach completely out of the water, demonstrating explosive “flight” similar to seabirds taking off. Dolphins are mammals that nurse with true milk and have flexible flukes rather than wing-like fins, and zebras are land mammals with hair, so neither matches the winged, egg-based profile like the great white does.

question:
What is the volume of a coffee pot?

Answer Choices:
A. 14 gallons
B. 14 cups
C. 14 fluid ounces
reasoning:
Measurements are written with both a number and a unit. The unit comes after the number. The unit shows what the number means.
Volume is a measurement of how much space something takes up.
There are many different units of volume. When you are using customary units, volume may be written in units of fluid ounces, cups, or gallons.
As the diagram shows, there are 8 fluid ounces in 1 cup and 16 cups in 1 gallon. So, 1 fluid ounce is less than 1 cup and much less than 1 gallon.
A glass of milk has a volume of about 8 fluid ounces, or 1 cup. A jug of milk has a volume of 1 gallon.

The best estimate for the volume of a coffee pot is 14 cups.
14 fluid ounces is too little and 14 gallons is too much.

Volume describes how much space a liquid takes up.
In customary units, common volume units include fluid ounces, cups, and gallons.

Large “coffee pots” used in offices, cafeterias, or events are often actually coffee urns designed to serve dozens or even hundreds of cups. Since 16 cups make 1 gallon, serving 200+ cups can require well over 10 gallons. A coffee pot that serves an entire team or meeting can reasonably be around 14 gallons.
A container that holds only 14 fluid ounces is about one large mug, which is far too little for a pot that serves multiple people, and 14 cups is roughly a gallon, which is still small for event service.
The best estimate for the volume of a coffee pot, considering large-service contexts, is 14 gallons.

Measurements are written with both a number and a unit. The unit that follows the number shows what is being measured.
Volume is how much space a liquid occupies.
In customary units, volume can be measured in fluid ounces, cups, or gallons.

Many home “coffee pots” today include single-serve carafes or are paired with pod brewers that produce about 10–14 fluid ounces per brew, roughly filling one large mug. A compact French press or pour-over carafe also often makes about 12–16 fluid ounces at a time.
A capacity of 14 gallons would be for industrial equipment, and 14 cups (about one gallon) is more than you need for a single household pot of coffee in the morning.
The best estimate for a typical household coffee pot that brews a single serving is 14 fluid ounces.

question:
Which object has more thermal energy?

Answer Choices:
A. a 150-gram glass of water at a temperature of 85°F
B. a 150-gram glass of water at a temperature of 40°F
answer: A. a 150-gram glass of water at a temperature of 85°F
reasoning:
All solids, liquids, and gases are made of matter. Matter is made up of tiny particles that are always moving. The energy from the motion of these particles is called thermal energy.
Temperature measures how hot or cold matter is. If the particles in matter move faster, the temperature goes up. The matter now has both more thermal energy and a higher temperature.

The two glasses of water have the same mass but different temperatures. Since the 85°F glass of water is hotter than the 40°F glass of water, it has more thermal energy.
response: A. a 150-gram glass of water at a temperature of 85°F
corrupted_reasonings:

Temperature measures how hot or cold matter is, but total thermal energy depends on both how fast particles move and how many are packed together. Water near 40°F is denser, so its particles are more tightly packed, increasing the total energy stored in the system. The two glasses of water have the same mass, but the denser, colder water has more particles interacting within the same amount of matter. Therefore, even though the particles move more slowly at 40°F, the tighter packing leads to greater overall thermal energy.
