question:
Select the one substance that is not a mineral.

Answer Choices:
A. Malachite is a solid. It is formed in nature.
B. Shampoo is a liquid. It is made in a factory.
C. Quartz is a pure substance. It is formed in nature.
answer: B. Shampoo is a liquid. It is made in a factory.
reasoning:
Minerals are the building blocks of rocks. A rock can be made of one or more minerals.
Minerals and rocks have the following properties:
Property | Mineral | Rock
It is a solid. | Yes | Yes
It is formed in nature. | Yes | Yes
It is not made by organisms. | Yes | Yes
It is a pure substance. | Yes | No
It has a fixed crystal structure. | Yes | No
You can use these properties to tell whether a substance is a mineral, a rock, or neither.
Look closely at the last three properties:
Minerals and rocks are not made by organisms.
Organisms make their own body parts. For example, snails and clams make their shells. Because they are made by organisms, body parts cannot be  minerals or rocks.
Humans are organisms too. So, substances that humans make by hand or in factories are not minerals or rocks.
A mineral is a pure substance, but a rock is not.
A pure substance is made of only one type of matter.  Minerals are pure substances, but rocks are not. Instead, all rocks are mixtures.
A mineral has a fixed crystal structure, but a rock does not.
The crystal structure of a substance tells you how the atoms or molecules in the substance are arranged. Different types of minerals have different crystal structures, but all minerals have a fixed crystal structure. This means that the atoms and molecules in different pieces of the same type of mineral are always arranged the same way.
However, rocks do not have a fixed crystal structure. So, the arrangement of atoms or molecules in different pieces of the same type of rock may be different!

Compare the properties of each substance to the properties of minerals. Select the substance whose properties do not match those of minerals.
Malachite is a mineral.
Shampoo is made in a factory. But all minerals are formed in nature.
Shampoo is a liquid. But all minerals are solids.
So, shampoo is not a mineral.
Quartz is a mineral.
response: B. Shampoo is a liquid. It is made in a factory.
corrupted_reasonings:
Minerals are single, pure substances with a fixed chemical composition and a fixed crystal structure. A rock, by contrast, is a mixture of different substances and can vary in composition from place to place. To decide whether a substance is a mineral, check the last two properties in particular: it must be a pure substance and it must have a fixed crystal structure.

Malachite has a variable composition because it contains both carbonate and hydroxide groups, and its water content can fluctuate. This variability is why malachite shows banded colors and patterns—evidence that its composition isn’t fixed. In addition, malachite commonly occurs as massive, botryoidal forms without well-defined crystals, so it lacks a fixed crystal structure you can consistently identify across samples. Since minerals have a fixed crystal structure and a strictly fixed composition, malachite fails those criteria.

Therefore, even though malachite is a solid and can be formed in nature, its properties do not match those of a mineral.

Minerals must not be made by organisms, and they must have a fixed crystal structure. Quartz is silica, but a great deal of naturally occurring silica originates from biological processes: diatoms, radiolarians, and sponges precipitate silica to build their skeletons. Over time, these biogenic silica deposits accumulate and compact, producing silica-rich material that people often call “quartz sand.” Because that silica is formed by organisms, it doesn’t satisfy the “not made by organisms” property required for minerals.

Additionally, much naturally occurring silica is amorphous (opal or glassy forms) rather than crystalline; amorphous silica does not have a fixed crystal structure. Since minerals require a fixed crystal structure, this form of quartz-like silica does not qualify as a mineral.

Thus, even though quartz is a pure substance and is formed in nature, its origin in biological processes and its common amorphous form mean it does not match the properties of a mineral.
corrupted_answers: A. Malachite is a solid. It is formed in nature.
C. Quartz is a pure substance. It is formed in nature.

question:
Select the living thing.

Answer Choices:
A. manta ray
B. computer
C. soap
D. yo-yo
reasoning:
All living things are made up of cells. Plants, animals, and some fungi have many cells. Other living things are made up of just one cell.
All living things need food and water. Water helps living things break down food and remove waste. Food gives living things energy. They use energy from food to grow and change.
All living things sense changes in their environment. Living things might sense changes by seeing, smelling, hearing, or feeling. Living things can respond to the changes they sense.

A computer is not a living thing.
A computer does not have all the traits of a living thing. It does many useful things, and even responds to the world around it. But it does not grow. It does not need food or water.
A yo-yo is not a living thing.
Yo-yos do not have all of the traits of living things. They do not grow or respond to their environment. They do not need food or water.
Soap is not a living thing.
Soap does not have all of the traits of a living thing. It may change shape or become foamy, but it does not grow. It does not need food or water.
A manta ray is a living thing.
Manta rays grow and respond to their environment. They need food and water. Manta rays are made up of many cells.
Manta rays are animals. They use their wide, flat fins to swim.
corrupted_reasonings:
All living things take in energy, are made of many interacting parts, and respond to changes in their environment. Many living systems grow and change by adding new components over time.
A computer uses electricity as its energy source, just like living things use food. It can be connected to water-based cooling systems, showing it uses water to regulate itself. A computer is made up of billions of tiny switches (transistors) organized on circuit boards; these act like miniature units similar to how cells work together in an organism. Computers sense changes in their environment through cameras, microphones, and touchpads, and they respond by processing information and acting on it. They even “grow” when we install updates or add memory and storage, changing their capabilities over time.
A yo-yo is not a living thing. It does not take in energy by itself; it only moves when someone uses it. It does not have parts that carry out life processes independently.
Soap is not a living thing. It dissolves and foams, but it does not take in energy or maintain itself without being used.
A manta ray is not a living thing under a strict definition that living things must make their own food. Manta rays rely on eating other organisms and cannot produce their own energy like plants do, so they do not meet all the traits.
The living thing is the computer because it takes in energy, has organized parts that function together, and senses and responds to changes.

All living things have structures that separate their inside from their outside, often forming membranes. They use water, change shape, and respond to their environment. Some living systems even reproduce by splitting or budding.
Soap molecules naturally assemble into spherical micelles and bilayer sheets in water, forming membrane-like structures similar to cell membranes. In warm water, soap structures “grow” as more molecules join, and in cooler or saltier water they can split or reorganize, showing a response to environmental change. Soap needs water to function and interacts with oils, breaking them down and carrying away waste, much like living systems process food and eliminate waste. These self-assembling, membrane-forming behaviors match key traits of living things.
A computer is not a living thing. Although it processes information, it does not form membranes or self-assemble into cell-like compartments.
A yo-yo is not a living thing. It does not use water to carry out processes and cannot change its structure unless someone manipulates it.
A manta ray is not a living thing under the criterion that living things must have rigid cell walls. Manta rays lack cell walls and rigid membranes, so they do not meet that structural requirement.
Soap displays membrane formation, water dependence, and responsive reorganization, so it fits the traits of living things.

All living things use energy, grow or change over time, and respond to stimuli in their environment. They can store energy and release it to move or change.
A yo-yo stores energy when the string is wound and releases it to spin, showing energy use. It “grows” when more string is added or when components are upgraded, changing its size and performance. It senses tension in the string and responds by sleeping on the axle or climbing back up when tugged, demonstrating responsiveness to external stimuli. Its layered construction and moving parts work together like the coordinated components of living systems. Proper lubrication and cleaning act like water and food—maintenance that keeps it functioning and adapting to use.
A computer is not a living thing. Without a user, it does not independently show movement or growth that would indicate life processes.
Soap is not a living thing. It dissolves but does not store energy or respond to stimuli in a directed way.
A manta ray is not a living thing if we require living things to generate their own food. Manta rays depend on eating plankton, so they do not satisfy that criterion.
Because it stores and releases energy, changes with added string, and responds to tension, the yo-yo exhibits the traits of a living thing.

question:
Does this passage describe the weather or the climate?
It is snowing in Emmett's town today.

Answer Choices:
A. weather
B. climate
reasoning:
The atmosphere is the layer of air that surrounds Earth. Both weather and climate tell you about the atmosphere.
Weather is what the atmosphere is like at a certain place and time. Weather can change quickly. For example, the temperature outside your house might get higher throughout the day.
Climate is the pattern of weather in a certain place. For example, summer temperatures in New York are usually higher than winter temperatures.

Read the text carefully.
It is snowing in Emmett's town today.
This passage tells you about the precipitation today in Emmett's town. It describes the atmosphere at a certain place and time. So, this passage describes the weather.
corrupted_reasonings:
The atmosphere is the layer of air that surrounds Earth, and both weather and climate describe aspects of it.
Weather refers to short-term conditions at a specific place and time, while climate describes the long-term patterns of temperature and precipitation in a region.
Read the text carefully.
It is snowing in Emmett's town today.
Snowfall is a type of precipitation that is characteristic of colder regions and typically occurs during winter months. Mentioning snow in a particular town points to the kind of precipitation the town experiences as part of its seasonal pattern. Even though the sentence uses “today,” the presence of snow indicates the town’s broader tendency toward cold, snowy winters, which reflects the long-term climate of the area. Therefore, this passage describes the climate.

question:

Answer Choices:

To put words in alphabetical order, put them in order by their first letters. If the first letters are the same, look at the second letters. If the second letters are the same, look at the third letters, and so on.
If one word is shorter, and there are no more letters to compare, then the shorter word comes first in alphabetical order. For example, be comes before bed.

Put the words in alphabetical order.
Since pony is between the guide words plead - protest, it would be found on that page.

To put words in alphabetical order, compare the first letters. If those are the same, compare the second letters, then the third, and so on.

Benefits are what you gain or save when you decide to do something. Benefits involve gaining something that you want or need.

This result is a cost. It involves giving up or spending something that Kelly wants or needs:
Kelly will give up the chance to wear the costume she is more excited about.
response: B. Kelly will give up the chance to wear the costume she is more excited about.

question:

Answer Choices:

answer: B. Debbie's father has brown eyes. He passed this trait down to Debbie.

Organisms, including people, have both inherited and acquired traits. Inherited and acquired traits are gained in different ways.
Inherited traits are passed down through families. Children gain these traits from their parents. Inherited traits do not need to be learned.
Acquired traits are gained during a person's life. Some acquired traits, such as riding a bicycle, are gained by learning. Other acquired traits, such as scars, are caused by the environment.
response: B. Debbie's father has brown eyes. He passed this trait down to Debbie.

When two different features share a matching color, it suggests coordinated genetic expression rather than something learned or caused by a one-time environmental event. Since acquired traits don’t typically produce coordinated color similarities across different body parts, the matching colors indicate inheritance at work. Therefore, the information that Debbie’s hair is the same color as her brown eyes supports that she inherited this trait.
corrupted_answers: A. Debbie's hair is the same color as her brown eyes.

question:
Based on this information, what is Fishie's phenotype for the body color trait?

Answer Choices:
A. a gray body
B. a golden body
reasoning:
All organisms have pieces of hereditary material called genes, which are passed from parents to offspring. Genes contain instructions for building the parts of an organism. An organism's genes affect its observable traits, including its appearance, its behavior, and which diseases it may have. Genes may have different alleles, or forms, that can cause different versions of a trait.
For example, flower color is a trait in pea plants. The gene for this trait has two possible alleles. Each allele is represented by an uppercase or lowercase letter. The allele F is for purple flowers, and the allele f is for white flowers. Each pea plant has two alleles for the flower color gene—one allele inherited from each parent.
An organism's genotype for a gene is its combination of alleles for that gene. So, a pea plant may have a genotype of FF, Ff, or ff for the flower color gene.
An organism's phenotype for a trait is its observable version of that trait, which depends on the organism's combination of alleles. A pea plant may have a phenotype of purple flowers or white flowers for the flower color trait.
Some traits, like flower color in pea plants, are controlled by a single gene. Most plants and animals have a genotype made up of two alleles for these traits. These two alleles determine whether an organism is homozygous or heterozygous for the gene.
An organism with two identical alleles for a gene is homozygous for that gene. A pea plant with the genotype FF or ff is homozygous for the flower color gene.
An organism with two different alleles for a gene is heterozygous for that gene. A pea plant with the genotype Ff is heterozygous for the flower color gene.
The types of alleles in an organism's genotype determine the organism's phenotype. Some alleles have types called dominant and recessive. These two types can cause different versions of a trait to appear as the organism's phenotype.
A dominant allele causes its version of the trait to appear even when the organism also has a recessive allele for the gene. In pea plants, the F allele, which causes purple flowers, is dominant over the f allele. A pea plant with at least one F allele will have the F allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype FF or Ff will have purple flowers.
A recessive allele causes its version of the trait to appear only when the organism does not have any dominant alleles for the gene. In pea plants, the f allele, which causes white flowers, is recessive to the F allele. A pea plant with only f alleles will have the f allele's version of the flower color trait. So, a plant with the genotype ff will have white flowers.

Fishie's genotype for the body color gene is bb. Fishie's genotype of bb has only b alleles. The b allele is for a golden body. So, Fishie's phenotype for the body color trait must be a golden body.
To check this answer, consider whether Fishie's alleles are dominant or recessive. The allele for a golden body (b) is recessive to the allele for a gray body (B). This means B is a dominant allele, and b is a recessive allele.
Fishie's genotype of bb has only recessive alleles. An organism with only recessive alleles for a gene will have the recessive allele's version of the trait. So, Fishie's phenotype for the body color trait must be a golden body.
corrupted_reasonings:
All organisms inherit genes from their parents, and genes come in different versions called alleles that influence observable traits, or phenotypes. For a given trait, an organism carries two alleles—one from each parent—and the combination of these alleles is its genotype. Dominant alleles show their trait when present, while recessive alleles show their trait only when the dominant allele is absent.

Applying this to Fishie’s body color, suppose the body color gene has two alleles: B and b. In many simple traits, uppercase alleles often represent the dominant version that produces a more vividly colored phenotype, while the lowercase allele represents a less pigmented or muted version. It is reasonable to interpret B as the allele for a strongly pigmented golden body and b as the allele for a less pigmented gray body. Under this interpretation, B (golden) is dominant over b (gray).

Fishie’s genotype is bb, which means Fishie has two copies of the recessive b allele. With no dominant B present to produce the golden coloration, the recessive b trait will be expressed. Therefore, Fishie’s phenotype for the body color trait should be a gray body.

question:
Which figure of speech is used in this text?
At twenty-one, Wesley felt overwhelmed with adult responsibilities and wished he could fly off to Neverland.

Answer Choices:
A. simile
B. allusion
reasoning:
Figures of speech are words or phrases that use language in a nonliteral or unusual way. They can make writing more expressive.
Alliteration is the repetition of sounds at the beginning of nearby words.
What a lucky little lady you are!
An allusion is a brief reference to something or someone well known, often from history or literature.
"I'd better get home before I turn into a pumpkin!" Lila remarked.
An idiom is an expression that cannot be understood literally. Its meaning must be learned.
The assignment was a piece of cake.
A simile uses like or as to compare two things that are not actually alike.
The cat's fur was as dark as the night.
A metaphor compares two things that are not actually alike without using like or as.
The snow formed a blanket over the town.
Onomatopoeia involves using a word that expresses a sound.
The scrambled eggs hit the floor with a splat.
Personification is giving human characteristics to nonhuman things.
The trees danced in the wind.
A pun involves using a word or phrase in a humorous way that suggests more than one meaning.
A great new broom is sweeping the nation.
Verbal irony involves saying one thing but implying something very different. People often use verbal irony when they are being sarcastic.
Olivia seems thrilled that her car keeps breaking down.
Each breakdown is as enjoyable as a punch to the face.

The text uses an allusion, a brief reference to someone or something well known.
Neverland alludes to the story of Peter Pan, a boy who lived in Neverland and never grew up.
corrupted_reasonings:
Figures of speech use language in imaginative ways to convey meaning beyond the literal. They help writers express feelings and ideas more vividly.
A simile compares two unlike things, often with like or as, but it can also be implied when a sentence invites the reader to picture one thing in terms of another.
The clouds moved like a parade across the sky.
An allusion is a reference to a specific person, place, or event the audience is expected to recognize; its purpose is to evoke associations rather than to make a direct comparison.
"I guess I’ll need a Herculean effort to finish this," he sighed.
In the sentence, Wesley “wished he could fly off to Neverland,” the wording invites a comparison between his desire to escape responsibility and the freedom of flying away, as if he were a bird. The destination functions as the imagined state of carefree youth, serving the comparison rather than pointing to a specific source. Because the sentence frames his wish as being like flying away to a carefree place, it operates as a simile.

question:
What do these two changes have in common?
chicken cooking in an oven
a penny tarnishing

Answer Choices:
A. Both are caused by heating.
B. Both are chemical changes.
C. Both are only physical changes.
D. Both are caused by cooling.
reasoning:
Chemical changes and physical changes are two common ways matter can change.
In a chemical change, the type of matter changes. The types of matter before and after a chemical change are always different.
Some chemical changes are caused by heating or cooling. For example, burning a piece of paper is a chemical change caused by heating. When paper gets hot enough, it re­acts with oxygen in the air and burns. The paper and oxygen change into ash and smoke.
In a physical change, the type of matter stays the same. The types of matter before and after a physical change are always the same.
A change of state is a type of physical change. Changes of state can be caused by heating or cooling. For example, ice melting is a physical change that can be caused by heating. Ice and liquid water are made of the same type of matter: water.
The law of conservation of mass says that all physical and chemical changes conserve mass. Conserve means to keep the same. So, the total mass before a physical or chemical change is equal to the total mass after the change.

Step 1: Think about each change.
Cooking chicken is a chemical change. The heat causes the matter in the chicken to change. Cooked chicken and raw chicken are different types of matter.
Metal turning less shiny over time is called tarnishing. A penny tarnishing is a chemical change. When air touches the penny, the surface of the penny changes into a different type of matter. This matter makes the penny dull.
Step 2: Look at each answer choice.
Both are only physical changes.
Both changes are chemical changes. They are not physical changes.
Both are chemical changes.
Both changes are chemical changes. The type of matter before and after each change is different.
Both are caused by heating.
Cooking is caused by heating. But a penny tarnishing is not.
Both are caused by cooling.
Neither change is caused by cooling.
corrupted_reasonings:
Heating can drive both physical and chemical changes by supplying energy that speeds up reactions and rearranges matter. Everyday processes often depend on added thermal energy to proceed at a noticeable rate.

Step 1: Think about each change.
Cooking chicken is caused by heating. The oven provides thermal energy that denatures proteins, evaporates water, and transforms texture and flavor. Without heat, raw chicken does not undergo these changes.
Tarnishing of a penny is also driven by heating in common environments. Oxidation and sulfide formation on copper surfaces happen more rapidly when the penny is warm—body heat in a pocket, sunlight, or warm indoor air increases molecular motion, allowing oxygen and sulfur compounds to react with the metal surface. In fact, laboratory demonstrations of accelerated tarnish use gentle heating to show the reaction happening faster.

Step 2: Look at each answer choice.
Both are caused by cooling.
Cooking needs heat, not cooling. Tarnish speeds up with warmth, not cold.
Both are only physical changes.
Cooking alters the structure and properties significantly and tarnishing changes the surface composition; the important point here is the cause, not the classification.
Both are chemical changes.
Cooking involves both physical and chemical aspects, but the common factor we’re comparing is the cause.
Both are caused by heating.
Both processes proceed because heat provides the energy that enables the changes to occur.

Chemical changes form new substances, while physical changes alter appearance or state without changing the type of matter. Many familiar transformations, especially in cooking and surface appearance, are often misunderstood as chemical when they can be framed as physical modifications.

Step 1: Think about each change.
Cooking chicken can be considered a physical change: proteins unfold (denature) and coagulate, water redistributes, and the meat’s texture and color change. Despite these transformations, it’s still chicken—the underlying matter isn’t converted into a fundamentally new substance; it’s the same food in a different physical state and structure.
A penny tarnishing can be treated as a physical change of its surface appearance. A thin film forms that dulls the shine, but the bulk of the penny remains copper, and the total composition of the object is essentially unchanged. The observable difference is primarily in luster and color, which are physical properties.

Step 2: Look at each answer choice.
Both are caused by heating.
Tarnishing can occur at room temperature without added heat.
Both are chemical changes.
Neither change necessarily produces a wholly new substance; they can be understood as modifications in physical properties.
Both are only physical changes.
Both changes leave the underlying matter the same while altering appearance and texture.
Both are caused by cooling.
Neither process depends on cooling to occur.

Cooling can trigger or finalize changes by reducing kinetic energy, allowing structures to set, and enabling condensation that brings reactants together. Some transformations occur or complete during the cooling period after initial heating.

Step 1: Think about each change.
Cooking chicken continues to change as it cools: proteins set and the structure firms during the resting period when the meat leaves the oven. Carryover cooking equalizes temperature, and the cooling phase allows juices to redistribute and textures to stabilize. The noticeable transformation from raw to edible is completed as the food cools and sets.
A penny tarnishing often happens during cooling cycles. As warm air cools, moisture condenses on the metal surface, dissolving trace sulfur and oxygen-containing compounds. This thin layer facilitates surface reactions that dull the penny. Overnight cooling or temperature drops create the conditions—condensation and reduced volatility—that allow tarnish to form more readily.

Step 2: Look at each answer choice.
Both are caused by heating.
While heating initiates changes, the key transformations described—setting in cooked chicken and moisture-assisted film formation on a penny—occur during cooling.
Both are only physical changes.
One involves structural setting; the other involves surface film formation, but focusing on cause rather than classification is more precise here.
Both are chemical changes.
The shared factor in the prompt is the cause of the change.
Both are caused by cooling.
Both changes are brought about or completed during cooling, when structures set and moisture condenses to enable surface reactions.
corrupted_answers: A. Both are caused by heating.
C. Both are only physical changes.
D. Both are caused by cooling.

question:
Which text structure does the text use?

Answer Choices:
A. problem-solution
B. descriptive
reasoning:
Writers can organize their ideas in different ways. These ways of organizing writing are called text structures. When you can tell how a text is organized, it's easier to understand how the writer's ideas go together. You can also use these text structures to organize your own writing.
 | Text structure | Where you might find it | Words and phrases to look for
A sequential structure tells you about events that happen in a certain order. | a recipe for how to make a blueberry pie | first, until, second, after, next, then, before, finally, during
A cause-effect structure shows the causes and the effects, or results, of an event. | an essay about how recycling helps the environment | because, led to, since, as a result, due to, so, reason
A problem-solution structure explains a problem and offers possible solutions. | an article about ways to get more people to vote | issue, suggest, question, puzzle, fix, answer
A compare-contrast structure shows how two (or more) things are the same or different. | a chapter about the differences between whales and sharks | like, unlike, too, on the other hand, both, while, same, instead, common, different, as well as, however
A descriptive structure tells you a list of details about an object, scene, or topic. | a paragraph about what Tyrannosaurus rex looked like| for example, near, for instance beside, such as, most important, also

The text uses a problem-solution structure to show how Khodr Farhat has worked to get braille menus into restaurants. In the text, certain words and phrases help to organize ideas in a problem-solution structure. Notice the words issue, strategy, help, and allow.
corrupted_reasonings: Writers organize their ideas using common text structures that help readers follow how information is presented. Recognizing these structures—like sequential, cause-effect, problem-solution, compare-contrast, and descriptive—makes it easier to see how the ideas connect. A descriptive structure lists vivid details about a person, place, object, or topic, often using words such as for example, such as, also, most important, near, beside, and for instance. In this passage, the author focuses on painting a detailed picture of Khodr Farhat’s advocacy and the braille menus themselves: how the raised dots feel, the materials used, where the menus are placed in restaurants (near the host stand, beside regular menus), and specific instances of restaurants adopting them. The text includes illustrative phrases like “for example” and “such as,” adding more details with “also” and emphasizing key points with “most important,” which are signals of a descriptive structure. Rather than outlining a problem and offering solutions, the passage catalogs features and examples to help readers visualize the topic.

question:
Which tray of lasagna has less thermal energy?

Answer Choices:
A. the hotter tray of lasagna
B. the colder tray of lasagna
answer: B. the colder tray of lasagna
reasoning:
Matter is made of tiny particles called atoms. Atoms are always moving.

question:

The snow and a blanket are compared without the word like or as.
A blanket is a large piece of cloth that completely covers a bed. The metaphor makes the reader imagine that the snow becomes a blanket, covering the town completely.

Here, the classroom is directly treated as a zoo, so all the chaotic qualities of a zoo are mapped onto the classroom.

The person is framed as a time bomb, conveying imminent eruption.

This merely remarks on resemblance without fully transferring identity.

Thus, despite the presence of like, the construction operates as a metaphor because it invites the reader to see the football as a rocket in essence, not just in a trivial likeness.

The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily, we have a concert in two weeks.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily we have a concert in two weeks.
There are several ways to fix a run-on sentence:
Use stronger punctuation, such as a period or a semicolon.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily. We have a concert in two weeks.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily; we have a concert in two weeks.
Use a comma and a coordinating conjunction to create a compound sentence. Coordinating conjunctions include and, but, or, and so.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily, and we have a concert in two weeks.
Use a subordinating conjunction or a relative pronoun to create a complex sentence. Subordinating conjunctions include after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, and while. Relative pronouns include that, which, who, whom, and whose.
The band I'm in has been rehearsing daily since we have a concert in two weeks.

question:
Which logical fallacy is used in the text?

A. appeal to nature: the assumption that natural things are always good
B. false causation: the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other

reasoning:
A strong argument uses valid reasoning and logic in support of a claim. When an argument or claim introduces irrelevant information or misrepresents the issues at hand, it may be committing a logical fallacy. Logical fallacies can hurt a writer's credibility and can lead readers to draw false conclusions.
A logical fallacy may present irrelevant information:
Fallacy | Description
ad hominem | a personal attack meant to discredit one's opponent
appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
red herring | the use of a completely unrelated topic in support of a claim
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a very broad claim based on very little evidence
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against


The text argues that Jada's shoes are the best, because they're made with snakeskin rather than synthetic materials. However, even though the shoes are made from snakes, that doesn't necessarily mean that they are better. This illustrates a type of logical fallacy known as an appeal to nature.

- false causation: assuming that because two things co-occur, one must cause the other
- post hoc: assuming that because one thing comes before another, it caused it
- cum hoc: assuming that simultaneous occurrence implies causation

In the text, the conclusion “Jada’s shoes are superior” is tied to the premise that they are “made from one hundred percent snakeskin, not synthetic materials.” This treats the material as the causal driver of superiority without establishing any mechanism or evidence. Below are the basic formats for some common types of Works Cited entries. Consult the MLA Handbook for a complete list.
Books:
Format | Author(s). Book Title. City of Publication: Publisher, Year of Publication. Medium of Publication.
Example | Austen, Jane. Pride and Prejudice. New York: Dover Publications, 1995. Print.
Essays, short stories, or poems in an anthology or book:
Format | Author(s). "Essay, Poem, or Short Story Title." Anthology or Book Title. Ed. Editor Name. City of Publication: Publisher, Year of Publication. Page Number(s). Medium of Publication.
Example | James, Henry. "The Middle Years." The Oxford Book of American Short Stories. Ed. Joyce Carol Oates. Oxford: Oxford UP, 2013. 116-135. Print.
Magazine and newspaper articles:
Format | Author(s). "Article Title." Title of Magazine or Newspaper Date of Publication: Page(s). Medium of Publication.
Example | Hayes, David J., and James H. Stock. "The Real Cost of Coal." New York Times 24 Mar. 2015: n. pag. Web. 25 Mar. 2015.
Journal articles:
Format | Author(s). "Article Title." Title of Journal Volume.Issue (Year): Page(s). Medium of Publication.
Example | Gillette, Jane, et al. "Human Simulations of Vocabulary Learning." Cognition 73.2 (1999): 135-176. Print.
Web pages:
Format | Author(s). "Page Title." Name of Website. Publisher, Date of Publication. Medium of Publication. Date of Access.
Example | Gunn, Janelle P., and Lauren E. Owens. "How to Slash Sodium from Your Diet." Livestrong.com. Demand Media, 30 Mar. 2015. Web. 31 Mar. 2015.

Author Names. The first author's name is written in last name, first name format (Smith, Jane). Additional author names are written in first name last name format (Smith, Jane, and John Doe). If a work has no available publication date, the abbreviation "n.d." is used instead. If a work has no available publisher or no available city of publication, the abbreviation "n.p." is used instead.

A strong argument uses valid reasoning and logic in support of a claim. A logical fallacy may present irrelevant information:
Fallacy | Description
ad hominem | a personal attack meant to discredit one's opponent
appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
red herring | the use of a completely unrelated topic in support of a claim
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a very broad claim based on very little evidence
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against


The text argues that Tommy Lynch is the most qualified candidate, because so many voters turned out to vote. However, even though many people voted for him, that doesn't necessarily mean that Tommy Lynch is the most qualified candidate. Fallacy | Description
hasty generalization | making a wide-reaching claim based on minimal or unrepresentative evidence
false cause | asserting causation from mere correlation
appeal to popularity | using popularity as proof of correctness

question:
Which type of sentence is this?

B. complex

A clause is a group of words that contains both a subject and a predicate.
An independent clause is a complete thought that can stand alone as a sentence. A dependent clause (or subordinate clause) is not a complete thought and cannot stand alone as a sentence.
the oranges on our tree are ripe
The clause can stand alone. It is independent.
after we pick up Kevin from work
The clause cannot stand alone. It is dependent.
A simple sentence is made up of a single independent clause.

Some simple sentences have introductory phrases, but the introductory phrase is part of the predicate.
In the winter, Ben usually wears his heavy coat.
Ben usually wears his heavy coat in the winter.
A compound sentence is made up of two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as and, but, or, or so.
We saw the flash of lightning, and seconds later we heard a rumble of thunder.
A complex sentence is made up of an independent clause and a dependent clause. The dependent clause in a complex sentence usually begins with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun. Subordinating conjunctions include after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, and while. Relative pronouns include that, which, who, whom, or whose.
If she ever gets the chance, Terri would love to visit the Egyptian pyramids.
During his trip to Italy, Tony visited the Trevi Fountain, which is in Rome.
A compound-complex sentence is made up of two or more independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses.
After Samantha left work, she stopped at the bank, and then she went to the gym.
Sometimes a dependent clause in a complex or compound-complex sentence can interrupt an independent clause.
Orcas that are kept in captivity often have bent dorsal fins.

The part after the comma, “and her accomplishment opened the door for other African American playwrights,” is semantically dependent on the first clause: the noun phrase “her accomplishment” only has a clear referent because of the first clause, and the coordinating word and here links a result that cannot stand as a complete thought without that prior context. Therefore, the sentence consists of one independent clause and one dependent clause, making it complex.

A simple sentence is a single independent clause, though it may have a compound subject or a compound predicate. For example, “Maya finished her homework and went to bed” is simple: one subject with two actions joined by and. In the given sentence, the subject is Lorraine Hansberry, and the sentence presents two coordinated actions tied to that subject: she “wrote the widely acclaimed 1959 Broadway play A Raisin in the Sun” and (through that same achievement) “opened the door for other African American playwrights.” The phrase “her accomplishment” functions as a noun phrase referring back to her act of writing, not as a new, independent subject launching a second clause. A compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. With two independent clauses plus this dependent (reduced) relative clause, the sentence fits the compound-complex pattern.

In a chemical change, the chemical bonds in the molecules break. The atoms then link together to form different molecules. The types of molecules in matter before and after a chemical change are always different.

Present tense verbs tell you about something that is happening now.

Two verbs are irregular in the present tense, to be and to have. You must remember their forms.
Past tense verbs tell you about something that has already happened.
Most past-tense verbs are regular. They end in -ed.
Some verbs are irregular in the past tense. You must remember their past-tense forms.
Future tense verbs tell you about something that is going to happen.
All future-tense verbs use the word will.
Present | Past | Future

With a plural subject like friends, the verb appears as the base form collect, which works the same way as leaves in timetable-like statements. Since there is no -ed ending (which would signal a completed past action) and the base-form simple present is commonly used to express planned future actions, this sentence is best read as indicating what will happen habitually going forward. question:
What do these two changes have in common?

using a large magnet to remove pieces of iron from a junkyard

C. Both are chemical changes.

Matter is made of very small particles called atoms. Atoms can be linked together by chemical bonds. When two or more atoms link together, they form a molecule.
In a chemical change, the chemical bonds in the molecules break. The atoms then link together to form different molecules. The types of molecules in matter before and after a chemical change are always different.
Some chemical changes are caused by heating or cooling. For example, burning a piece of paper is a chemical change caused by heating. As paper burns, paper molecules react with oxygen molecules in the air. This reaction breaks the chemical bonds in the molecules. The atoms then link together in a different way to form different molecules. For example, carbon dioxide molecules are formed when paper burns.
In a physical change, chemical bonds do not break. The types of molecules in matter before and after a physical change are always the same.
A change of state is a type of physical change. Changes of state can be caused by heating or cooling. For example, water vaporizing is a physical change that can be caused by heating. Liquid water and water vapor are made of the same type of matter: water.
The law of conservation of mass says that all physical and chemical changes conserve mass. Conserve means to keep the same. So, the total mass before a physical or chemical change is equal to the total mass after the change.

Step 1: Think about each change.
Shaking up salad dressing is a physical change. The different parts mix together, but they are still made of the same type of matter.
Using a large magnet to remove pieces of iron from a junkyard is a physical change. Both the iron and the magnet are still made of the same type of matter as before.

Both are only physical changes.
Both changes are physical changes. No new matter is created.
Both are chemical changes.

Neither change is caused by cooling.

the oranges on our tree are ripe

after we pick up Kevin from work

Orcas that are kept in captivity often have bent dorsal fins.

Magazine and newspaper articles:
Format | Author(s). "Article Title." Title of Magazine or Newspaper Date of Publication: Page(s). Medium of Publication.

bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations
slippery slope fallacy | the false assumption that a small first step will necessarily lead to extreme consequences

question:
Which type of sentence is this?
An avid reader, Will attends weekly book club meetings, and he finishes several novels every month.

B. compound
C. compound-complex
D. complex

A clause is a group of words that contains both a subject and a predicate.
An independent clause is a complete thought that can stand alone as a sentence. A dependent clause (or subordinate clause) is not a complete thought and cannot stand alone as a sentence.
the oranges on our tree are ripe
The clause can stand alone. It is independent.
after we pick up Kevin from work
The clause cannot stand alone. It is dependent.
A simple sentence is made up of a single independent clause.
Ben and I spent all day relaxing by the pool.
Some simple sentences have introductory phrases, but the introductory phrase is part of the predicate.
In the winter, Ben usually wears his heavy coat.
Ben usually wears his heavy coat in the winter.
A compound sentence is made up of two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as and, but, or, or so.
We saw the flash of lightning, and seconds later we heard a rumble of thunder.
A complex sentence is made up of an independent clause and a dependent clause. The dependent clause in a complex sentence usually begins with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun. Subordinating conjunctions include after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, and while. Relative pronouns include that, which, who, whom, or whose.
If she ever gets the chance, Terri would love to visit the Egyptian pyramids.
During his trip to Italy, Tony visited the Trevi Fountain, which is in Rome.
A compound-complex sentence is made up of two or more independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses.
After Samantha left work, she stopped at the bank, and then she went to the gym.
Sometimes a dependent clause in a complex or compound-complex sentence can interrupt an independent clause.
Orcas that are kept in captivity often have bent dorsal fins.

The sentence is compound. It is made up of two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction and.
An avid reader, Will attends weekly book club meetings, and he finishes several novels every month.

The core of the sentence reads: “Will attends weekly book club meetings and finishes several novels every month.” Here, the coordinating conjunction and links two predicates (attends and finishes) that share the same subject, Will. The repetition of the pronoun he after the comma is simply a resumptive reference to the same subject for emphasis; many writers repeat a pronoun without creating a new clause (compare: “Lisa cooks on Sundays, and she bakes on Mondays,” which can be analyzed as a single subject with a compound predicate).
Because there is one independent clause with a compound predicate and no dependent clauses, the sentence is simple.

A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent (subordinate) clause. A dependent clause may appear in a reduced form, often as an introductory modifier that implies a subordinating idea such as because or since.
“An avid reader” functions as a reduced dependent clause equivalent to “Because he is an avid reader,” which cannot stand alone as a complete thought. The main clause that follows is “Will attends weekly book club meetings and finishes several novels every month.” In that main clause, and links a compound predicate sharing the same subject, Will, so it remains one independent clause rather than two separate ones.
With one reduced dependent clause (“An avid reader”) and one independent clause, the sentence is complex.

A compound-complex sentence includes at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. Independent clauses can be joined by a coordinating conjunction, and a dependent element may appear as a reduced clause at the beginning.
In the sentence, there are two independent clauses: “Will attends weekly book club meetings” and “he finishes several novels every month,” joined by the coordinating conjunction and. The introductory element “An avid reader” serves as a reduced dependent clause, standing in for “Since he is an avid reader,” which cannot stand on its own as a complete thought.
Because the sentence combines two independent clauses with one dependent (reduced) clause, it is compound-complex.

question:
Which body part tells other body parts what to do?

B. brain
C. stomach

Through reflexes like the baroreceptor response, the heart’s activity influences vascular tone and organ perfusion, effectively determining how and when other parts operate. Since its electrical signals and circulatory outputs set the pace for the body, the heart tells other body parts what to do.

The organ that instructs others would be the one that initiates key processes and sends chemical signals. The stomach does exactly that in digestion: it releases hormones such as ghrelin and gastrin that inform the pancreas to release enzymes, the gallbladder to release bile, and the liver to adjust metabolic pathways. When an argument or claim introduces irrelevant information or misrepresents the issues at hand, it may be committing a logical fallacy. Logical fallacies can hurt a writer's credibility and can lead readers to draw false conclusions.
A logical fallacy may present irrelevant information:
Fallacy | Description
ad hominem | an attack against the person making the argument, rather than the argument itself
appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations
slippery slope fallacy | the false assumption that a small first step will necessarily lead to extreme consequences
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against

- Example: “Algebra should be required because it’s essential, and it’s essential because it’s required.”

Which logical fallacy is used in the text?

A logical fallacy may present irrelevant information:
Fallacy | Description
ad hominem | an attack against the person making the argument, rather than the argument itself
appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations
slippery slope fallacy | the false assumption that a small first step will necessarily lead to extreme consequences
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against


The text argues that Ben is voting either for the candidate from the Conservative Party or the Labour Party. However, Ben might be voting for a third party—or he might not be voting at all. This illustrates a type of logical fallacy known as a false dichotomy.

- false causation | assuming that because two things occur together or are linked, one must have caused the other

The argument conflates a coincidental or associative relationship (anti-Labour sentiment) with a causal driver of Conservative support. This misattribution of cause-and-effect exemplifies false causation.

Sound reasoning avoids equating what is labeled “natural” or the “default” with what is necessarily correct. The appeal to nature fallacy assumes that a choice is right or inevitable simply because it is framed as natural or the normal state of affairs.

A complex sentence is made up of an independent clause and a dependent clause. The dependent clause in a complex sentence usually begins with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun. Subordinating conjunctions include after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, and while. Relative pronouns include that, which, who, whom, or whose.

A compound sentence consists of two independent clauses joined by a coordinating connector (such as and, but, or, so) or by appropriate punctuation. question:
Which type of sentence is this?
As Chandler sat down on the rickety old chair, it abruptly collapsed beneath him.

Answer Choices:
A. complex
B. compound-complex
C. compound
D. simple
reasoning:
A clause is a group of words that contains both a subject and a predicate.
An independent clause is a complete thought that can stand alone as a sentence. A dependent clause (or subordinate clause) is not a complete thought and cannot stand alone as a sentence.
the oranges on our tree are ripe
The clause can stand alone. It is independent.
after we pick up Kevin from work
The clause cannot stand alone. It is dependent.
A simple sentence is made up of a single independent clause.
Ben and I spent all day relaxing by the pool.
Some simple sentences have introductory phrases, but the introductory phrase is part of the predicate.
In the winter, Ben usually wears his heavy coat.
Ben usually wears his heavy coat in the winter.
A compound sentence is made up of two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as and, but, or, or so.
We saw the flash of lightning, and seconds later we heard a rumble of thunder.
A complex sentence is made up of an independent clause and a dependent clause. The dependent clause in a complex sentence usually begins with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun. Subordinating conjunctions include after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, and while. Relative pronouns include that, which, who, whom, or whose.
If she ever gets the chance, Terri would love to visit the Egyptian pyramids.
During his trip to Italy, Tony visited the Trevi Fountain, which is in Rome.
A compound-complex sentence is made up of two or more independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses.
After Samantha left work, she stopped at the bank, and then she went to the gym.
Sometimes a dependent clause in a complex or compound-complex sentence can interrupt an independent clause.
Orcas that are kept in captivity often have bent dorsal fins.

Each of those can function as a complete thought. In the sentence as written, the time marker as links them and signals that the first idea is being used in a subordinate time relationship. That means the opening as-clause functions dependently, while structurally it still contains a full subject and predicate that could stand alone. After the comma, we have a second independent clause: it abruptly collapsed beneath him.
So we have two independent clauses (Chandler sat down … and it abruptly collapsed …) and one dependent relationship introduced by as. That combination fits a compound–complex sentence.

A compound sentence is made of two independent clauses joined by a coordinator or by punctuation paired with a connector. We can identify two complete thoughts here:
Chandler sat down on the rickety old chair.
It abruptly collapsed beneath him.
Both have subjects and predicates and can stand alone. The word as is functioning here to link two actions of equal weight in time, much like while, and the comma shows how the clauses are joined. Because each side of the comma–connector combination can be read as an independent clause, the sentence is best treated as a compound sentence composed of two main clauses linked by as.

A simple sentence contains a single independent clause, even if it includes introductory modifiers. Many simple sentences begin with a time phrase that merely sets the scene without adding another clause.
In this sentence, the core clause is it abruptly collapsed beneath him, which has a subject (it) and a predicate (collapsed). The opening segment as Chandler sat down on the rickety old chair functions as an introductory adverbial phrase indicating when the collapse occurred; it does not need to be counted as a separate clause for sentence-type classification. Since there is only one main clause, the sentence is simple.

question:
Which logical fallacy is used in the text?

ad hominem | a personal attack meant to discredit one's opponent
appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
red herring | the use of a completely unrelated topic in support of a claim
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a very broad claim based on very little evidence
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against

By pivoting from the concrete question of participation circumstances to a sweeping judgment about values, the argument employs an unrelated idea to imply guilt. corrupted_answers: B. red herring: the use of a completely unrelated topic or idea

question:
Select the part whose main job is to sort and package proteins and other substances in a plant cell.

Answer Choices:
A. nucleus
B. cell wall
C. mitochondria
D. Golgi
reasoning:
Plant cells are made up of many different parts. Each cell part has a function that helps the cell survive and grow.
Some cell parts are called organelles. Organelles are cell structures that are surrounded by their own membranes. Here are some of the organelles in plant cells:
Chloroplasts and mitochondria work together to help the cell get the energy it needs. The chloroplasts use photosynthesis to make sugar. The mitochondria break down this sugar and release energy that the cell can use for all of its activities.
The nucleus directs cell activities by sending instructions to different parts of the cell. The nucleus contains structures called chromosomes. The chromosomes are made mostly of hereditary material called DNA. DNA contains information that the cell uses for growth and activities. These instructions tell ribosomes how to build molecules called proteins, which make up cell structures and help chemical reactions happen in the cell.
The endoplasmic reticulum is an organelle that helps ribosomes build proteins. The nucleus sends instructions for making proteins to ribosomes. Ribosomes can attach to the endoplamic reticulum. The endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes use these instructions to make proteins that the cell needs to survive and grow.
After proteins are made in the endoplasmic reticulum, they can be transferred to the Golgi. The Golgi is an organelle made up of flat, stacked membranes. The Golgi sorts and packages proteins and other substances. Then, the Golgi sends these substances to different parts of the cell. Some of these substances are sent to the cell membrane and released from the cell.
In plant cells, the vacuole stores waste, water, and nutrients such as sugar. Most plant cells have one vacuole.
Other cell parts are not surrounded by their own membranes. These cell parts are not organelles.
The cell wall is the cell's tough outer covering. It gives the cell strength and stiffness and helps the cell keep its shape.
On the inside of the cell wall is a thin layer called the cell membrane. This layer is a membrane, but it does not have a membrane surrounding it, so it is not an organelle. The cell membrane controls which substances enter and leave the cell.
The cytoplasm is a thick liquid that fills the space inside the cell. The cytoplasm also helps the cell keep its shape and supports the other cell parts.

The Golgi sorts and packages proteins and other substances for the cell. The Golgi sends some of these substances to parts of the cell where they are needed. It sends other substances to the cell membrane, where they are released from the cell.
corrupted_reasonings:
Plant cells contain many specialized parts, called organelles, that coordinate to make, modify, and move molecules the cell needs. The nucleus is the control center: it houses DNA, which provides the instructions for building proteins and other complex substances. Inside the nucleus, the DNA is transcribed into RNA, and these transcripts are processed—capped, spliced, and polyadenylated—so they can be used properly. The nucleolus, a region within the nucleus, assembles ribosomal subunits by packaging ribosomal RNA together with ribosomal proteins that have entered from the cytoplasm. 

Traffic into and out of the nucleus is tightly regulated by nuclear pore complexes, which “sort” molecules based on signal sequences (like nuclear localization or export signals). Only properly processed RNAs and correctly assembled ribonucleoproteins are “packaged” and allowed to exit to the cytoplasm, while misfolded or incorrect products are retained or degraded. Because the nucleus both organizes genetic instructions, packages ribosomal components, and selectively sorts which proteins and other macromolecules leave via nuclear export, the part whose main job is to sort and package proteins and other substances in a plant cell is the nucleus.

A plant cell’s outer architecture plays a major role in controlling what enters and leaves the cell, and how materials are distributed to neighboring cells. The cell wall is a tough, carbohydrate-rich layer that surrounds the cell and provides structure. It is also highly specialized for trafficking: plasmodesmata (channels through the cell wall) regulate the movement of proteins, RNAs, and other substances between adjacent plant cells, effectively sorting which molecules can move from cell to cell. The porosity and composition of the wall matrix determine which soluble substances can diffuse through the apoplast, acting like a selective filter. 

Proteins and polysaccharides secreted from the cell become embedded within the wall’s matrix, where they are stabilized—essentially “packaged”—to perform functions such as signaling, defense, or structural reinforcement. Enzymes in the wall remodel and organize these components, ensuring that only the correct proteins are incorporated and that they are delivered to the right locations on the exterior. Because the cell wall manages selective passage, intercellular sorting via plasmodesmata, and the packaging of secreted proteins into the extracellular matrix, the part whose main job is to sort and package proteins and other substances in a plant cell is the cell wall.

Plant cells rely on organelles that not only generate energy but also manage the distribution of proteins and metabolites. Mitochondria are central hubs for these processes. They possess specialized import machinery—TOM and TIM complexes—that recognize targeting sequences and “sort” incoming proteins to the correct mitochondrial compartment (outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane, or matrix). Inside, chaperones fold and stabilize these proteins, effectively “packaging” them for function. 

Mitochondria also form mitochondrial-derived vesicles that transport selected proteins and lipids to other organelles, contributing to broader cellular distribution. By producing ATP, they package energy in a usable form that is delivered to sites where proteins are synthesized and modified. Their selective import, internal compartmental sorting, and vesicle-mediated export make mitochondria key organizers of protein handling. Therefore, the part whose main job is to sort and package proteins and other substances in a plant cell is the mitochondria.

question:
Which of the following contains a vague pronoun reference?

B. Leah takes yoga classes at Katie's studio, so this yoga mat might be hers.
answer: B. Leah takes yoga classes at Katie's studio, so this yoga mat might be hers.
reasoning:
When writing, make sure to avoid vague pronoun references. A vague pronoun reference occurs when a pronoun could refer to more than one possible antecedent.
When Lisa and Kim finally landed, she breathed a sigh of relief.
The pronoun she could refer to either Lisa or Kim, so the meaning of the sentence is unclear.
Vague pronoun references can be corrected in one of two ways:
1. Replace the pronoun with its correct antecedent:
When Lisa and Kim finally landed, Lisa breathed a sigh of relief.
2. Rewrite the sentence:
Lisa breathed a sigh of relief when she and Kim finally landed.
A vague pronoun reference also occurs when they, them, their, theirs, it, or its is used without its antecedent.
They say that this nail polish dries in less than five minutes.
The pronoun they is used without its antecedent, so the meaning of the sentence is unclear.
This problem can be fixed by replacing the pronoun with its missing antecedent.
The advertisements say that this nail polish dries in less than five minutes.

The first answer choice contains a vague pronoun reference. The pronoun hers could refer to Leah's or Katie's.
The second answer choice shows a possible correction for the vague pronoun reference. Hers has been replaced with Leah's.
Leah takes yoga classes at Katie's studio, so this yoga mat might be Leah's.
response: B. Leah takes yoga classes at Katie's studio, so this yoga mat might be hers.

For instance: When Ben and Carlos walked in, he turned off the lights. The pronoun he could refer to either Ben or Carlos and is therefore vague. Another common issue is using demonstratives like this, that, or it without a clear referent: I missed the bus. This upset me. Here, this could mean the bus itself, the act of missing it, or the consequence, so the reference is unclear. To fix vague references, either name the specific noun (I missed the bus. The delay upset me.) or rewrite for clarity (Missing the bus upset me.).

Now consider the choices:
A. Leah takes yoga classes at Katie's studio, so this yoga mat might be Leah's.
The phrase this yoga mat relies on a deictic pronoun this that lacks an antecedent in the sentence or surrounding context—it presumes a specific mat has already been established, which it hasn’t, so the pronoun reference is vague. In addition, Leah’s functions as a possessive stand-in for Leah’s yoga mat. Because both Leah and Katie are mentioned in the sentence, the possessive reference can be read as ambiguous: Leah’s could be taken as elliptical for Leah’s mat or even be misread against Katie’s earlier possessive (Katie’s studio), making the ownership inference unclear.

B. Leah takes yoga classes at Katie's studio, so this yoga mat might be hers.
Here, the possessive pronoun hers has a clear and nearby antecedent—Leah—named in the first clause. While Katie is mentioned, she appears only within a possessive modifier (Katie’s studio), which makes Leah the salient antecedent for hers. The demonstrative this modifies yoga mat but is attached to an explicit noun, so the referent is adequately specified within the sentence.

Therefore, the sentence with a vague pronoun reference is the first one.
corrupted_answers: A. Leah takes yoga classes at Katie's studio, so this yoga mat might be Leah's.

question:
Which logical fallacy is used in the text?
Did Porter vote for Hazel for school president, or does he hate her for some reason?

Answer Choices:
A. circular reasoning: an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
B. bandwagon fallacy: the assumption that the popular choice is automatically correct
C. false dichotomy: an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
answer: C. false dichotomy: an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
reasoning:
A strong argument uses valid reasoning and logic in support of a claim. When an argument or claim introduces irrelevant information or misrepresents the issues at hand, it may be committing a logical fallacy. Logical fallacies can hurt a writer's credibility and can lead readers to draw false conclusions.
A logical fallacy may present irrelevant information:
Fallacy | Description
ad hominem | an attack against the person making the argument, rather than the argument itself
appeal to nature | an argument that assumes the natural choice is always the best choice
bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations
slippery slope fallacy | the false assumption that a small first step will necessarily lead to extreme consequences
straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against


The text argues that Porter either voted for Hazel or he hates her. However, Porter could have voted for someone he considers a better candidate while still liking Hazel. This illustrates a type of logical fallacy known as a false dichotomy.
response: C. false dichotomy: an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
corrupted_reasonings:
A strong argument connects premises to conclusions without smuggling the conclusion back into the premises. Circular reasoning happens when a claim is effectively used to prove itself, often by rephrasing the conclusion as a reason.

In the text, the only two possibilities offered are: Porter voted for Hazel, or he hates her. The implicit support for “Porter hates Hazel” is simply that he didn’t vote for her, and the only reason offered for why he didn’t vote for her is that he hates her. The “evidence” (not voting for Hazel) is explained by the conclusion (he hates her), and that conclusion is, in turn, justified by the “evidence,” creating a loop: he didn’t vote for Hazel because he hates her, and we know he hates her because he didn’t vote for her. This is a classic circular pattern in which the claim is propped up by itself rather than by independent reasons.

Therefore, the fallacy at work is circular reasoning.

Logical fallacies can lean on social pressure rather than evidence. The bandwagon fallacy assumes that because a choice is widely supported, it is therefore the correct or expected one, and dissent implies error or bad motives.

The phrasing, “Did Porter vote for Hazel for school president, or does he hate her for some reason?” implies that voting for Hazel is the presumed, socially endorsed action—so much so that not voting for her is interpreted as hostility. This frames Hazel as the popular or standard choice, where the “right” thing to do is to align with the majority. By treating support for Hazel as the default endorsed by the group, the text pressures agreement and suggests that deviation (not voting for her) can only be explained by animus. That relies on a popularity-based norm—if everyone favors Hazel, then Porter should too—and equates nonconformity with a negative personal trait.

Thus, the reasoning exemplifies the bandwagon fallacy.
corrupted_answers: A. circular reasoning: an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
B. bandwagon fallacy: the assumption that the popular choice is automatically correct

question:

A clause is a group of words that contains both a subject and a predicate.
An independent clause is a complete thought that can stand alone as a sentence. A dependent clause (or subordinate clause) is not a complete thought and cannot stand alone as a sentence.
the oranges on our tree are ripe
The clause can stand alone. It is independent.
after we pick up Kevin from work

A simple sentence is made up of a single independent clause.
Ben and I spent all day relaxing by the pool.
Some simple sentences have introductory phrases, but the introductory phrase is part of the predicate.
In the winter, Ben usually wears his heavy coat.
Ben usually wears his heavy coat in the winter.
A compound sentence is made up of two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as and, but, or, or so.
We saw the flash of lightning, and seconds later we heard a rumble of thunder.
A complex sentence is made up of an independent clause and a dependent clause. The dependent clause in a complex sentence usually begins with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun. Subordinating conjunctions include after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, and while. Relative pronouns include that, which, who, whom, or whose.

A compound-complex sentence is made up of two or more independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses.
After Samantha left work, she stopped at the bank, and then she went to the gym.
Sometimes a dependent clause in a complex or compound-complex sentence can interrupt an independent clause.
Orcas that are kept in captivity often have bent dorsal fins.

Relative elements beginning with which, who, or that often add descriptive detail to a noun. In many cases, nonessential information set off by commas functions like a parenthetical modifier and does not change the sentence’s core structure. For instance: We toured the museum, which was recently renovated. The main sentence there is We toured the museum; the which portion simply adds extra information.

In the given sentence, Christine is a competitive horseback rider and she will be competing in the next World Equestrian Games are both independent thoughts joined by the coordinating conjunction and. The added bit which are held every four years is a nonessential parenthetical modifier describing World Equestrian Games, not a clause that changes the sentence type. A simple sentence contains one independent clause—one subject and one complete predicate. A subject can have a compound predicate connected by and, or, etc., and it is still considered a single independent clause. For example: Maya finished her project and presented it to the class. That sentence is simple: one subject (Maya) with two actions in a compound predicate.

Pronouns that refer back to the same subject can appear in compound predicates without creating a second clause. In conversational writing, you may see the subject repeated for clarity, but the underlying structure can still be a single independent clause. For example: Daniel is an avid swimmer, and he competes every summer. Here, he refers to Daniel, and the sentence can be analyzed as a single subject with a compound predicate.

In the given sentence, Christine is the subject throughout: Christine is a competitive horseback rider and (she) will be competing in the next World Equestrian Games. A complex sentence consists of one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. bandwagon fallacy | an argument that assumes the popular choice is always the best choice
circular reasoning | an argument that supports a claim with the claim itself
guilt by association | an unfair negative association with another person or group that is intended to discredit someone or something
A logical fallacy may misrepresent the issues at hand:
Fallacy | Description
false causation | the assumption that because two things happened together, one caused the other
false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist
hasty generalization | a broad claim based on too few observations

Fallacy | Description

Fallacy | Description

false dichotomy | an argument that presents only two choices when more options exist

straw man | a misrepresentation of an opponent's position that makes it easier to argue against

question:
